ocar.opportunity: Animal behavior is shaped both by evolution and by individual experience. Parallel brain pathways encode innate and learned valences of cues, so mapping how those signals meet is a route to understanding action selection.
ocar.challenge: How innate and learned valences are integrated during action-selection is not well understood.
ocar.action: Eschbach and colleagues used electron microscopy in Drosophila larva to map, at synaptic resolution, all neurons downstream of mushroom-body output neurons and to characterize their interactions with lateral-horn neurons.
ocar.resolution: The map revealed multiple convergence neuron types that receive both mushroom-body and lateral-horn input. A subset is excited by positive-valence mushroom-body and lateral-horn pathways and inhibited by negative-valence mushroom-body pathways; two of these neurons encode integrated odor value and bidirectionally regulate turning.
ocar.future_work: The authors speculate that learning could skew excitation and inhibition onto these neurons and thereby modulate turning, a prediction that remains to be tested.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly larvae have both built-in likes and dislikes and the ability to learn new ones. This paper maps how those two kinds of value meet in the brain so the animal can decide whether to turn toward or away from a smell.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2021), Eschbach and colleagues used electron microscopy of Drosophila larva to map every neuron downstream of mushroom-body output cells, which carry learned value, and to see how they mix with lateral-horn cells that carry innate value. They found several types of convergence neurons; some are excited by positive-valence pathways and inhibited by negative-valence mushroom-body pathways. Two of those cells encode combined odor value and can increase or decrease turning.
summaries.advanced: The reconstruction is comprehensive for neurons downstream of all mushroom-body output neurons in this larval electron-microscopy volume, but functional connectivity and behavioral roles are confirmed for only two of the identified cells. The idea that learning skews excitation–inhibition balance to modulate turning is explicitly speculative. The work is grounded in one Drosophila larva volume and does not by itself establish the same architecture in adults or other species.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly larvae have both built-in likes and dislikes and the ability to learn new ones. This paper maps how those two kinds of value meet in the brain so the animal can decide whether to turn toward or away from a smell.

ocar.opportunity: Nanoscale connectomics now produces automated and semi-automated wiring diagrams from terabytes and petabytes of dense three-dimensional neuroimagery. Rapid quality assessment would promote analysis and reuse of those products.
ocar.challenge: Connectome generation involves imperfect steps including dense three-dimensional segmentation, anisotropic nonrigid alignment, and pixel classification of neurons and synapses. As volumes grow, the community still lacks scalable ways to assess reconstruction quality.
ocar.action: Bishop and colleagues share CONFIRMS, a scalable toolkit that assesses connectome quality via targeted inquiry and large-scale graph analysis, illustrated on a recent electron-microscopy reference dataset.
ocar.resolution: The toolkit is intended both to score reconstructions as black-box products and to suggest how proofreading processes might be improved. The authors also note clinical relevance of large-scale electron microscopy for disease characterization if reconstruction bottlenecks are overcome.
ocar.future_work: A natural next step is to use such assessments to optimize proofreading and to apply the same black-box checks as connectome generation becomes more commonplace.

summaries.beginner: Brain wiring maps are now built by computers from huge stacks of microscope images, but those maps can still contain mistakes. This paper shares a toolkit for checking a finished wiring map without having to reopen every processing step.
summaries.intermediate: At EMBC (2021), Bishop and colleagues introduced CONFIRMS, a scalable toolkit for assessing automated electron-microscopy connectomes as black-box products. Reconstruction involves imperfect segmentation, alignment, and synapse classification on terabyte- to petabyte-scale volumes. CONFIRMS uses targeted inquiry and large-scale graph analysis, illustrated on a recent reference dataset, both to score quality and to inform proofreading.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name the reference dataset or report numerical accuracy scores, so the toolkit’s operating characteristics must be judged from the full paper. Clinical claims are framed as future possibility once reconstruction bottlenecks are overcome, not as a demonstrated medical application.

plain_language_summary: Brain wiring maps are now built by computers from huge stacks of microscope images, but those maps can still contain mistakes. This paper shares a toolkit for checking a finished wiring map without having to reopen every processing step.

ocar.opportunity: Since the Cambrian, animals diversified from a few body plans into many species, each served by a characteristic neural architecture. Comparative whole-brain maps could reveal which circuits are shared and which diverged.
ocar.challenge: How the connectome of each animal differs from closely related species, or whether it converged onto an optimal architecture shared with more distant ones, is unknown.
ocar.action: Barsotti, Correia, and Cardona review how advances in molecular biology, microscopy, storage, processing, and computational neuroscience have lowered barriers to whole-brain connectomics, and they argue for comparative maps of small representative species across the phylogenetic tree.
ocar.resolution: They propose that such comparisons can infer the archetypal neural architecture of each body plan and identify circuits that may have converged onto a shared, potentially optimal structure.
ocar.future_work: The review frames comparative connectomics of suitable small species as the next practical step, not a completed reconstruction program.

summaries.beginner: Different animal body plans come with different brain layouts, but we still do not know which wiring patterns are unique and which evolved more than once. This review argues that mapping complete small brains across many species is now becoming possible.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), Barsotti, Correia, and Cardona argue that whole-brain connectomics is newly practical because of advances in molecular biology, microscopy, data handling, and computational neuroscience. They propose mapping relatively small representative species across the phylogenetic tree. The goal is to infer archetypal architectures for each body plan and to spot circuits that may have converged on a shared structure.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/review, not a new dataset: no species list, reconstruction counts, or empirical comparisons are given in the abstract. Claims about ‘optimal’ architectures are hypotheses to be tested by future comparative maps.

plain_language_summary: Different animal body plans come with different brain layouts, but we still do not know which wiring patterns are unique and which evolved more than once. This review argues that mapping complete small brains across many species is now becoming possible.

ocar.opportunity: Quantitative synaptic ultrastructure is a basis for estimating the relative strength of transmission across circuits. Electron microscopy remains the gold standard for visualizing synaptic morphology in three dimensions.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing long dendritic segments and their spines from serial-section transmission electron microscopy requires an unimaginable amount of effort and time. Conventional light microscopy cannot resolve synaptic junctions with the same certainty.
ocar.action: Parajuli and Koike review studies that determined three-dimensional synapse ultrastructure, with a focus on dendritic-spine synapses in the rodent brain, and they discuss automated volume electron microscopy tools that make such reconstructions more realistic.
ocar.resolution: The review synthesizes work on spine structural diversity, organization along dendrites, presynaptic wiring patterns, and activity-dependent remodeling.
ocar.future_work: Automated imaging has addressed low throughput only to an appreciable degree; scaling from individual spines to long dendritic arbors remains the practical frontier.

summaries.beginner: Tiny bumps on nerve-cell branches, called spines, are where many brain connections sit. This review explains how three-dimensional electron-microscope pictures have shown the shapes of those connections and how they change with activity.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2021), Parajuli and Koike review volume electron microscopy of dendritic-spine synapses, especially in rodent brain. They contrast light microscopy of putative junctions with electron microscopy as the gold standard, and they note that serial-section transmission electron microscopy can reconstruct synapses but is too slow for long dendrites. Automated imaging tools now make dendritic-segment reconstruction more realistic. The review covers spine diversity, dendritic organization, presynaptic wiring, and activity-dependent remodeling.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new reconstruction: it does not report original counts or a named volume. The focus is rodent dendritic spines, so generalizations to other synapse classes or taxa are not established here. Serial-section TEM remains the reference method in the narrative even as automated volume tools are highlighted.

plain_language_summary: Tiny bumps on nerve-cell branches, called spines, are where many brain connections sit. This review explains how three-dimensional electron-microscope pictures have shown the shapes of those connections and how they change with activity.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic segmentation and synapse prediction in electron-microscopy brain volumes now make nanometer-scale neuron reconstructions possible. A synapse-resolution connectivity graph is a tool for understanding the nervous system in health and disease.
ocar.challenge: Automatic segmentation sometimes fails on large neurons, and general proofreading requires inspecting large volumes at the pixel level, which is visually intensive and time-consuming.
ocar.action: Gonda and colleagues designed VICE, an analytics framework that streamlines proofreading of connectivity-related errors using automated likely-error detection, synapse clustering, and interactive three-dimensional visualization, focused on the local circuit of a single cell.
ocar.resolution: A user study with quantitative and subjective feedback found the framework more efficient for proofreading, for understanding evolving graphs, and for sharing error-correction strategies.
ocar.future_work: The local-circuit completeness strategy invites extension to larger circuits and to other error classes beyond connectivity-related mistakes.

summaries.beginner: Computers can now trace nerve cells in microscope volumes, but they still make mistakes that people must fix by eye. This paper presents a visual tool that points people toward likely connection errors around one cell at a time.
summaries.intermediate: In Computer Graphics Forum (2021), Gonda, Wang, Beyer, Hadwiger, Lichtman, and Pfister introduce VICE, a proofreading framework for electron-microscopy connectomes. Automatic segmentation often fails on large neurons, so the system uses likely-error detection and synapse clustering plus interactive three-dimensional views, centering on one cell’s local circuit. A user study reported that people found it more efficient for correcting errors, tracking evolving graphs, and sharing strategies.
summaries.advanced: The abstract reports user-study conclusions but no numerical error-rate reductions. The strategy deliberately targets connectivity-related errors and local-circuit completeness rather than exhaustive pixel-level correction of an entire volume. Transfer beyond the studied users and datasets is not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Computers can now trace nerve cells in microscope volumes, but they still make mistakes that people must fix by eye. This paper presents a visual tool that points people toward likely connection errors around one cell at a time.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic image segmentation and synapse prediction in electron-microscopy datasets now enable more efficient reconstruction of neural connectivity. Combining machine guidance with human three-dimensional reasoning could accelerate that work.
ocar.challenge: A single neuron can span thousands of images with complex arbors and thousands of synapses. Algorithms excel in narrow fields of view but sometimes fail on large neurons that need more context, whereas humans are comparatively good at reasoning about large objects.
ocar.action: Hubbard and colleagues introduce semi-automated strategies in a tool called Neu3 that combine three-dimensional visualization with merge and cleaving operations driven by affinity scores in the underlying segmentation.
ocar.resolution: They report superior performance compared with prior work, enabling more efficient reconstruction of much larger datasets, and they extract proofreading insights about trade-offs when tuning segmentation parameters.
ocar.future_work: The affinity-driven merge and split workflows are positioned to scale reconstruction as volumes grow, with parameter choices informed by the proofreading trade-offs they clarify.

summaries.beginner: Computers are good at tracing tiny pieces of nerve cells but often lose the big picture of a whole cell. This preprint describes a three-dimensional tool that lets people quickly glue or split those pieces using scores from the computer’s own map.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Hubbard and colleagues describe Neu3, a reconstruction tool that pairs three-dimensional visualization with machine-guided merge and cleaving along supervoxel boundaries, driven by segmentation affinities. Automatic methods struggle with large neurons that need wide context, while humans handle those objects better. The authors report better performance than prior work and discuss how proofreading experience should tune segmentation parameters.
summaries.advanced: The abstract claims superior performance without naming the comparison methods or reporting numerical speed or accuracy gains. The work is a preprint methods paper; generalization to particular organisms or named public volumes is not stated here.

plain_language_summary: Computers are good at tracing tiny pieces of nerve cells but often lose the big picture of a whole cell. This preprint describes a three-dimensional tool that lets people quickly glue or split those pieces using scores from the computer’s own map.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics datasets now describe brain structure at the level of individual synaptic connections and continue to grow in size and complexity. Searching for graph patterns is a promising way to reduce dimensionality and enable discovery.
ocar.challenge: These graphs are often too large to analyze manually, creating barriers to searching for structure and testing hypotheses.
ocar.action: Matelsky and colleagues combine graph databases and analysis libraries with a neuroscience-oriented query grammar, DotMotif, so researchers can construct queries and search for subgraphs without solving the underlying computer-science problems themselves.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate motif search on simulated data and real public connectomics datasets and share example structures relevant to neuroscience.
ocar.future_work: The authors provide software and case studies intended to motivate future exploration at the scale of nanoscale brain networks.

summaries.beginner: Modern brain wiring maps are huge networks that are hard to search by hand. This paper offers an open tool that lets scientists ask, in a neuroscience-friendly language, whether a small wiring pattern appears in those maps.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2020), Matelsky and colleagues introduce DotMotif, pairing graph databases with a query grammar designed for nanoscale brain networks. Connectomes are too large for manual pattern search, so the tool abstracts graph-theory challenges. They demonstrate motif queries on simulated data and public connectomics datasets and share example structures.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name the public datasets or report motif counts or runtime benchmarks. DotMotif is a search and query layer, not a new reconstruction; results depend on the quality of the input graph.

plain_language_summary: Modern brain wiring maps are huge networks that are hard to search by hand. This paper offers an open tool that lets scientists ask, in a neuroscience-friendly language, whether a small wiring pattern appears in those maps.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping neuroanatomy is a foundational goal toward understanding brain function. Light microscopy could add molecular cell-type information that electron microscopy reconstructions often lose.
ocar.challenge: Electron microscopy is the gold standard for connectivity because nanoscale resolution is needed to resolve synapses unambiguously, but molecular information that specifies cell types is often lost. Light microscopy has lacked that nanoscale resolution.
ocar.action: Shen and colleagues develop spectral connectomics: multicolor Brainbow labeling combined with multi-round immunostaining expansion microscopy (miriEx) to interrogate morphology, molecular markers, and connectivity in the same brain section.
ocar.resolution: They link inhibitory neuron types with their morphologies and show that correlative Brainbow and synaptic-machinery immunostaining can define putative synaptic connections and map putative inhibitory and excitatory inputs.
ocar.future_work: They envision routine application in neurobiology labs to study normal and pathophysiological neuroanatomy; the connections remain putative rather than ultrastructurally confirmed synapses.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopes can see individual brain connections but often lose the molecular labels that say which cell types they are. This paper uses colorful genetic labels plus a swelling trick so a light microscope can map likely connections and cell types in the same tissue.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2020), Shen, Harrington, Walker, Cheng, Boyden, and Cai introduce spectral connectomics: Brainbow multicolor labeling plus multi-round immunostaining expansion microscopy (miriEx). Electron microscopy remains the gold standard for synapses but often loses molecular identity. The method links inhibitory cell types to morphology and uses synaptic-machinery staining to define putative connections and excitatory versus inhibitory inputs.
summaries.advanced: Synapses identified this way are explicitly putative, not electron-microscopy-confirmed contacts. The abstract does not name a brain region, species beyond the general method context, or quantitative comparison of false-positive rates against electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopes can see individual brain connections but often lose the molecular labels that say which cell types they are. This paper uses colorful genetic labels plus a swelling trick so a light microscope can map likely connections and cell types in the same tissue.

ocar.opportunity: Emerging neuroimaging datasets from electron microscopy, optical microscopy, or X-ray microtomography describe neurons and connections at unprecedented scale. Standard, reproducible pipelines would let more laboratories work with those data.
ocar.challenge: Modern imaging quickly accumulates gigabytes to petabytes, and many laboratories lack resources: computer-vision tools are often not portable or scalable, and reproducing or extending methods is difficult.
ocar.action: Johnson and colleagues developed an ecosystem of open-source neuroimaging pipelines with standardized modules, applied as exemplars to synapse-level connectomes from electron microscopy and to cell distributions from X-ray microtomography.
ocar.resolution: They propose a generalized processing framework that connects existing open-source projects for large-scale storage, reproducible algorithms, and workflow execution, arguing that approaches can be standardized across neuroimaging experiments.
ocar.future_work: The techniques are demonstrated on neuroimaging datasets but may be applied to similar problems in other domains.

summaries.beginner: New microscopes produce enormous pictures of brain tissue that many labs cannot process with their own computers. This paper offers a shared, open set of processing pipelines so those pictures can be turned into maps in a repeatable way.
summaries.intermediate: In GigaScience (2020), Johnson and colleagues describe an open-source ecosystem for volumetric nanoscale neuroimaging. Datasets from electron microscopy, optical microscopy, or X-ray microtomography reach gigabytes to petabytes, but tools are often not portable. Exemplars include synapse-level connectomes from electron microscopy and cell distributions from X-ray microtomography, tied together by storage, reproducible algorithms, and workflow engines.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name specific public volumes or report accuracy metrics for the exemplar pipelines. Portability claims are architectural; laboratory-by-laboratory resource gaps remain a stated motivation rather than a measured outcome.

plain_language_summary: New microscopes produce enormous pictures of brain tissue that many labs cannot process with their own computers. This paper offers a shared, open set of processing pipelines so those pictures can be turned into maps in a repeatable way.

ocar.opportunity: Most connectome reconstruction pipelines first predict affinities and run watershed, then merge over-segmented regions. Adding global and biological context could refine those over-segmentations.
ocar.challenge: Current methods rely only on local context and are typically agnostic to underlying biology. A few merge errors can incorrectly join several neuronal processes, so algorithms are tuned toward over-segmentation that creates a costly proofreading burden.
ocar.action: Matejek and colleagues add a third pipeline step: extract a graph of potential split errors, prune it with biologically inspired geometric constraints and two neural networks that learn neuronal shapes, then merge by graph partitioning that uses global context.
ocar.resolution: On four real-world connectomics datasets they report an average variation-of-information improvement of 21.3%.
ocar.future_work: The approach is positioned to increase throughput for large-scale reconstruction by reducing over-segmentation that would otherwise require proofreading.

summaries.beginner: Computer programs that trace nerve cells in microscope images often cut cells into too many pieces so they do not accidentally glue the wrong cells together. This paper adds a later step that uses the overall shape of neurons to decide which pieces should be joined.
summaries.intermediate: At CVPR (2019), Matejek and colleagues propose a third reconstruction stage after affinity prediction, watershed, and local merging. They build a graph of possible split errors, shrink it with morphology-based geometric constraints and two neural networks that learn neuronal shapes, then partition the graph using global context. On four real-world connectomics datasets they report an average variation-of-information improvement of 21.3%.
summaries.advanced: The 21.3% figure is an average across four unnamed datasets in the abstract; per-dataset scores and comparison methods are not given here. The method still starts from an over-segmentation and therefore inherits errors that cannot be expressed as missing merges along the extracted graph.

plain_language_summary: Computer programs that trace nerve cells in microscope images often cut cells into too many pieces so they do not accidentally glue the wrong cells together. This paper adds a later step that uses the overall shape of neurons to decide which pieces should be joined.

ocar.opportunity: Isotropic high-resolution imaging of large volumes would advance connectomics and cell biology. Conventional focused-ion-beam scanning electron microscopy offers high resolution, robust alignment, and few artifacts for tracing neurites.
ocar.challenge: Prevailing deficiencies in imaging speed and duration cap the maximum possible FIB-SEM image volume.
ocar.action: Xu, Pang, Hayworth, and Hess developed technologies that expand FIB-SEM volume by more than four orders of magnitude, from 10^3 µm^3 to 3 × 10^7 µm^3, while maintaining 8 × 8 × 8 nm^3 voxels, with an option to trade speed for 4 × 4 × 4 nm^3 voxels.
ocar.resolution: The enhanced platform is described as capable of years of continuous imaging without defects in the final stack, supporting connectomic tracing of fine neurites and generating organelle ground truth for machine learning.
ocar.future_work: Primarily limited by time, the maximum volume can be greatly extended; the preprint details operating-parameter optimization based on resolution and electron-dose constraints.

summaries.beginner: A special electron microscope can shave and photograph tissue in very even three-dimensional detail, which is excellent for following thin nerve fibers, but it used to be too slow for large pieces of brain. This paper describes upgrades that make much larger volumes practical.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2019), Xu, Pang, Hayworth, and Hess report enhanced FIB-SEM that expands image volume by more than four orders of magnitude, from 10^3 µm^3 to 3 × 10^7 µm^3, at 8 × 8 × 8 nm^3 voxels. Conventional FIB-SEM already offered high isotropic resolution and robust alignment but was limited in speed and duration. Trading speed yields 4 × 4 × 4 nm^3 voxels for organelle ground truth. They describe years-scale continuous imaging without defects in the final stack.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name a biological specimen for the expanded volumes. ‘Years of continuous imaging without defects’ is a reliability claim for the platform as described, not an independent audit. Higher-resolution 4 nm operation is explicitly a speed trade-off.

plain_language_summary: A special electron microscope can shave and photograph tissue in very even three-dimensional detail, which is excellent for following thin nerve fibers, but it used to be too slow for large pieces of brain. This paper describes upgrades that make much larger volumes practical.

ocar.opportunity: A complete synaptic map of one antennal-lobe glomerulus would be a resource for Drosophila olfactory circuitry, including local interneurons that had been elusive.
ocar.challenge: Local interneurons in glomerulus VA1v had been difficult to reconstruct fully, and genetic screens of projection neurons may not have reached saturation.
ocar.action: Horne and colleagues used FIB-SEM to densely reconstruct all neurons in glomerulus VA1v of the right antennal lobe in Drosophila melanogaster, including local interneurons.
ocar.resolution: Fruitless-positive, sexually dimorphic VA1v included more than 11,140 presynaptic sites with about 38,050 postsynaptic dendrites, connecting 51 ipsilateral and 56 contralateral olfactory receptor neurons, 18 projection neurons, and 56 of more than 150 previously reported local interneurons. A matrix of 192 bodies each with more than 50 connections accounts for 88% of the glomerulus’s pre- and postsynaptic sites.
ocar.future_work: Projection neurons were more numerous than genetic screens suggested, implying those screens had not saturated; the dense matrix is offered as a community resource.

summaries.beginner: One small pocket in the fruit-fly smell center mixes incoming smell cells, local cells, and outgoing cells. This paper uses a three-dimensional electron microscope to list essentially every connection inside that pocket.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2018), Horne and colleagues densely reconstructed glomerulus VA1v of the right Drosophila antennal lobe with FIB-SEM. They report more than 11,140 presynaptic sites and about 38,050 postsynaptic dendrites among 51 ipsilateral and 56 contralateral olfactory receptor neurons, 18 projection neurons, and 56 local interneurons. Olfactory receptor neurons are mostly presynaptic and projection neurons mostly postsynaptic; local circuits confer extensive reciprocity except for LN2V. A 192-body matrix with more than 50 connections each covers 88% of sites.
summaries.advanced: The map is one glomerulus on the right side of one fly, not the whole antennal lobe. Local interneuron coverage is 56 of more than 150 previously reported types, so completeness is relative to this glomerulus, not the full local-interneuron census. Connection counts come from a thresholded matrix of bodies with more than 50 connections.

plain_language_summary: One small pocket in the fruit-fly smell center mixes incoming smell cells, local cells, and outgoing cells. This paper uses a three-dimensional electron microscope to list essentially every connection inside that pocket.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic image segmentation is critical to scale electron-microscopy connectome reconstruction. Better metrics and software would make evaluation useful for large datasets and downstream analysis.
ocar.challenge: Competitions such as CREMI and SNEMI often fail to capture challenges of larger datasets because ground truth is time-consuming. Common metrics do not emphasize downstream analysis, miss connectivity, and can over-rate segmentation quality.
ocar.action: Plaza and Funke introduce metrics aligned with reconstruction use—including synapse connectivity and completeness, plus unsupervised orphan-fragment and self-loop measures—and a scalable software framework with visualization for comparing segmentations.
ocar.resolution: They evaluate the framework on two relatively large public ground-truth datasets and report novel insights on example segmentations.
ocar.future_work: The ecosystem is intended for practical evaluation of large datasets in both supervised and unsupervised settings.

summaries.beginner: When computers trace cells in brain microscope images, scores that only look at pixels can make a map look better than it is for following real connections. This paper proposes new scores, some of which do not even need a human-drawn answer key, and software to compute them at large scale.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2018), Plaza and Funke argue that CREMI- and SNEMI-style contests miss large-dataset challenges and that standard metrics can over-rate segmentations because they ignore connectivity. They propose synapse connectivity and completeness metrics, plus unsupervised measures based on orphan fragments and self-loops. A scalable software framework integrates metrics and debugging visualizations, evaluated on two relatively large public ground-truth datasets.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name the two public datasets or report numerical metric values. Unsupervised orphan and self-loop measures still require interpretation: they flag failure modes rather than prove biological correctness.

plain_language_summary: When computers trace cells in brain microscope images, scores that only look at pixels can make a map look better than it is for following real connections. This paper proposes new scores, some of which do not even need a human-drawn answer key, and software to compute them at large scale.

ocar.opportunity: A synaptic map of the neurons that underlie food intake would show how sensory paths reach feeding motor, modulatory, and neuroendocrine outputs in Drosophila larvae.
ocar.challenge: How monosynaptic and polysynaptic sensory routes are organized onto common motor outputs in a feeding circuit was not mapped at whole-central-nervous-system scale.
ocar.action: Miroschnikow and colleagues reconstructed, from a whole-central-nervous-system electron-microscopy volume, the synaptic map of input and output neurons for larval food intake.
ocar.resolution: Input neurons from enteric, pharyngeal, and external organs converge onto seven distinct sensory synaptic compartments. Monosynaptic connections from a set of those compartments cover motor, modulatory, and neuroendocrine targets in overlapping domains, with polysynaptic routes superimposed so divergent sensory paths reconverge. A different set of compartments connects to the mushroom-body calyx, whose outputs reach interneurons that target feeding output neurons.
ocar.future_work: The architecture of converging monosynaptic and multisynaptic paths is offered as a template for further functional tests of feeding control.

summaries.beginner: Eating requires the brain to combine many taste and gut signals and then drive chewing, swallowing, and internal messengers. This paper traces those paths in a fruit-fly maggot from a complete electron-microscope map of its central nervous system.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2018), Miroschnikow and colleagues reconstructed larval Drosophila feeding inputs and outputs from a whole-central-nervous-system electron-microscopy volume. Sensory neurons from enteric, pharyngeal, and external organs converge on seven synaptic compartments. Monosynaptic links from a subset of compartments cover feeding motor, serotonergic, and neuroendocrine cells in overlapping domains, with polysynaptic routes on top. Separate compartments reach the mushroom-body calyx, whose outputs contact interneurons onto feeding outputs.
summaries.advanced: The map is anatomical: the abstract does not report physiology or behavior that tests the inferred converging paths. Completeness is claimed for the reconstructed feeding-related input and output neurons in this larval volume, not for every interneuron in the larva.

plain_language_summary: Eating requires the brain to combine many taste and gut signals and then drive chewing, swallowing, and internal messengers. This paper traces those paths in a fruit-fly maggot from a complete electron-microscope map of its central nervous system.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics extracts brain connectivity graphs from electron-microscopy images using machine learning and image processing. High-throughput processing matched to microscope pace would make connectomes available on demand.
ocar.challenge: The field had assumed that processing would require mass storage, CPU/GPU farms, and months or years. A competing trend treats distributed MapReduce-style clusters as a substitute for careful algorithm and performance engineering.
ocar.action: Matveev and colleagues present a high-throughput connectomics-on-demand system that runs on a multicore machine with fewer than 100 cores, as a case study in algorithms, parallelization, and performance engineering.
ocar.resolution: They report extraction of connectomes at the terabyte-per-hour pace of modern electron microscopes on that single commodity-class machine.
ocar.future_work: The result is offered as evidence that cluster-scale problems can sometimes be solved on one multicore machine if the software is engineered accordingly.

summaries.beginner: People often assume that turning huge microscope movies of brain tissue into wiring maps requires a warehouse of computers and months of waiting. This paper shows a carefully engineered program that can keep up with a modern microscope on one powerful desktop-class machine.
summaries.intermediate: At PPoPP (2017), Matveev and colleagues argue against treating distributed CPU/GPU clusters as a replacement for algorithm and performance engineering. They built a connectomics-on-demand pipeline on a multicore machine with fewer than 100 cores. They report extracting connectomes at the terabyte-per-hour pace of modern electron microscopes.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name the dataset, reconstruction accuracy, or which pipeline stages are included in the terabyte-per-hour figure. ‘Fewer than 100 cores’ is an upper bound, not a measured core count. Throughput is matched to microscope pace rather than compared numerically with a named cluster baseline here.

plain_language_summary: People often assume that turning huge microscope movies of brain tissue into wiring maps requires a warehouse of computers and months of waiting. This paper shows a carefully engineered program that can keep up with a modern microscope on one powerful desktop-class machine.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic cell-image segmentation in connectomics produces merge and split errors that require proofreading. Speeding the visual search for those errors would accelerate correction.
ocar.challenge: Previous research identified visual search for errors as the bottleneck in interactive proofreading.
ocar.action: Haehn and colleagues train two convolutional-network classifiers on automatic-segmentation errors versus expert ground truth to recommend candidate merges and splits, so users can correct with yes/no decisions; they also present a fully automatic thresholded mode.
ocar.resolution: They report that corrections reduce variation of information 7.5× faster than previous proofreading methods. Experiments with automatic mode and with novice versus expert users compare favorably with state-of-the-art methods on different connectomics datasets.
ocar.future_work: Guided recommendations could be extended as a standard interactive or automatic proofreading stage across datasets.

summaries.beginner: When a computer traces cells, it sometimes glues two cells together or splits one cell apart, and finding those mistakes by eye is slow. This paper trains a helper that points to likely mistakes so a person can say yes or no.
summaries.intermediate: At CVPR (2018; work dated 2017 in the record), Haehn, Kaynig, Tompkin, Lichtman, and Pfister train convolutional networks on segmentation errors versus expert labels to propose merges and splits using a large context around boundaries. Users then make yes/no corrections, which the authors report reduces variation of information 7.5× faster than previous proofreading methods. A fully automatic thresholded mode is also presented, with novice and expert user experiments on multiple connectomics datasets.
summaries.advanced: The 7.5× speedup is relative to unnamed previous methods in the abstract. Dataset names and absolute remaining error rates are not given here. Automatic mode still depends on choosing a probability threshold.

plain_language_summary: When a computer traces cells, it sometimes glues two cells together or splits one cell apart, and finding those mistakes by eye is slow. This paper trains a helper that points to likely mistakes so a person can say yes or no.

ocar.opportunity: Defining organizational principles of neuronal networks at the cellular scale—micro-connectomics—is a key challenge of modern neuroscience. Graph theory, often informed by economical principles that go back to Cajal’s conservation laws, offers a language for those principles.
ocar.challenge: It remains to evaluate whether cellular-scale networks reflect an economical trade-off between biological cost and functional value.
ocar.action: Schröter, Paulsen, and Bullmore review graph-theoretical parameters of micro-connectome topology from intact small organisms and from samples of larger nervous systems.
ocar.resolution: Various results suggest that many aspects of neuronal network organization are the outcome of competition between biological cost and functional value.
ocar.future_work: The review frames further tests of that economical trade-off as the way to interpret new cellular-scale maps.

summaries.beginner: Even a tiny piece of nervous system is a network of cells, and scientists want simple rules for how those networks are arranged. This review asks whether brains wire themselves as a compromise between keeping costs down and keeping function up.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2017), Schröter, Paulsen, and Bullmore survey graph-theoretical descriptions of cellular-scale connectomes, drawing on Cajal-style conservation ideas. They summarize studies in intact small organisms and in samples from larger nervous systems. They argue that much of the organization looks like a trade-off between biological cost and functional value.
summaries.advanced: This is a review of topology, not a new reconstruction. Evidence for an economical trade-off is described as ‘various results suggest,’ not as a single decisive test. Micro-connectomes from samples of large brains are incomplete relative to whole-animal maps.

plain_language_summary: Even a tiny piece of nervous system is a network of cells, and scientists want simple rules for how those networks are arranged. This review asks whether brains wire themselves as a compromise between keeping costs down and keeping function up.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics now images brain tissue at nanometer resolution, producing petabytes that must be aligned, labeled, proofread, and formed into graphs. Each step requires visualization for human verification.
ocar.challenge: Massive data volumes make interactive visualization and application development difficult without a middleware layer that hides low-level data wrangling.
ocar.action: Haehn and colleagues present BUTTERFLY, a scalable middleware that outputs image and geometry suitable for hardware-accelerated rendering and supports Web-based applications across the connectomics workflow.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate open-source applications for data management, queries, two- and three-dimensional visualization, interactive editing, and graph analysis, and they measure and optimize rendering throughput from storage to display.
ocar.future_work: They share design recommendations for open-source data-management and visualization platforms in everyday connectomics research.

summaries.beginner: Nanometer-scale brain images are so large that even looking at them smoothly is a software problem. This paper describes a middle layer that helps websites and tools show, edit, and analyze those pictures without each program reinventing data handling.
summaries.intermediate: In Informatics (2017), Haehn and colleagues introduce BUTTERFLY middleware for petabyte-scale connectomics visualization. Alignment, labeling, proofreading, and graph formation all need human visual checks. The platform feeds hardware-accelerated rendering and underpins Web apps for storage, queries, two- and three-dimensional views, editing, and graph analysis, with measured rendering throughput.
summaries.advanced: The abstract reports design and throughput optimization but no user-study accuracy metrics. Scalability claims are tied to the demonstrated application series rather than a named production volume size here.

plain_language_summary: Nanometer-scale brain images are so large that even looking at them smoothly is a software problem. This paper describes a middle layer that helps websites and tools show, edit, and analyze those pictures without each program reinventing data handling.

ocar.opportunity: Neurosecretory centers use peptidergic signaling to influence physiology and behavior. Mapping cell types, synapses, and peptidergic networks is required to understand those centers.
ocar.challenge: An entire neurosecretory center had not been reconstructed jointly for synaptic and peptidergic connectivity.
ocar.action: Williams and colleagues used transmission electron microscopy and gene-expression mapping in larval Platynereis dumerilii to reconstruct 78 neurosecretory neurons and map their synaptic connectivity, then analyzed peptide–receptor pairs in spatially mapped single-cell transcriptomes.
ocar.resolution: The anterior center expresses many neuropeptides, including hypothalamic peptide orthologs and their receptors. Peptide–receptor pairs form sparsely connected networks linking specific neuronal subsets. Experimental analysis of one pair showed that a neuropeptide can couple neurosecretory and synaptic brain signaling.
ocar.future_work: The study uncovers extensive peptidergic networks within a neurosecretory center and its connection to the synaptic brain, inviting similar overlays in other species.

summaries.beginner: Some brain cells talk not only through wired contacts but also by releasing chemical messengers that drift to other cells. This paper maps both the wires and the messenger systems in a hormone-like control center of a marine worm larva.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2017), Williams and colleagues reconstructed 78 neurosecretory neurons in the larval Platynereis brain with transmission electron microscopy and gene-expression mapping. The anterior center expresses many neuropeptides, including hypothalamic orthologs and receptors. Spatially mapped transcriptomes showed sparse peptide–receptor networks, and one experimentally tested pair coupled neurosecretory and synaptic signaling.
summaries.advanced: Peptidergic links inferred from expression of peptide–receptor pairs are not the same as observed synapses; only one pair is experimentally analyzed. The reconstruction is 78 neurosecretory neurons in one larval brain, not the entire Platynereis nervous system.

plain_language_summary: Some brain cells talk not only through wired contacts but also by releasing chemical messengers that drift to other cells. This paper maps both the wires and the messenger systems in a hormone-like control center of a marine worm larva.

ocar.opportunity: Analysing computations in neural circuits often uses simplified models because the actual implementation is unknown. Motion detection has long been described by Hassenstein–Reichardt or Barlow–Levick models.
ocar.challenge: Those models simulate motion detection well, but the exact neuronal circuits remain elusive.
ocar.action: Takemura and colleagues reconstructed a comprehensive connectome of Drosophila motion-sensing T4 cell circuits using a novel electron-microscopy technique.
ocar.resolution: Putative excitatory inputs cluster at T4 dendrite shafts and inhibitory inputs at the bases. Mi1 and Tm3 provide most synaptic contacts onto T4, but the authors could not reproduce a previously reported spatial offset between those cells. The map includes candidate anatomical substrates for both Hassenstein–Reichardt and Barlow–Levick detectors.
ocar.future_work: The unresolved spatial-offset discrepancy with prior work is a concrete target for further anatomy and physiology.

summaries.beginner: How the eye senses motion has been described with simple textbook diagrams for decades, but the real cells behind those diagrams were incomplete. This paper traces the wiring onto motion-sensing cells in the fruit fly in great detail.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2017), Takemura, Nern, Chklovskii, Scheffer, Rubin, and Meinertzhagen reconstructed Drosophila T4 motion circuits with a novel electron-microscopy method. Putative excitatory inputs cluster on T4 dendrite shafts and inhibitory inputs at their bases. Mi1 and Tm3 still provide most synapses onto T4, but a previously reported spatial offset between Mi1 and Tm3 could not be reproduced. The connectome offers candidate substrates for both Hassenstein–Reichardt and Barlow–Levick detectors.
summaries.advanced: Failure to reproduce the Mi1–Tm3 spatial offset is an explicit conflict with prior work and limits simple two-input detector stories. Excitatory versus inhibitory labels on inputs are described as putative. Completeness is claimed for T4 circuits in this reconstruction, not for the entire optic lobe.

plain_language_summary: How the eye senses motion has been described with simple textbook diagrams for decades, but the real cells behind those diagrams were incomplete. This paper traces the wiring onto motion-sensing cells in the fruit fly in great detail.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics aims to reconstruct three-dimensional neuron morphology from electron-microscopy images. Convolutional networks have succeeded at membrane segmentation, but high-throughput synapse identification is still needed for connectivity graphs.
ocar.challenge: There has been comparatively little success in high-throughput identification of intercellular synaptic connections required for deriving connectivity graphs.
ocar.action: Santurkar and colleagues take a compositional approach: train lighter networks on membranes, clefts, and vesicles from 100 electron-microscopy samples, then combine feature maps with biology-derived heuristics instead of asking a deep net to learn all combinations.
ocar.resolution: They report 7% higher recall and 5% higher F1-score than previous state of the art, a 20-fold speed-up versus previous fastest implementations, and reconstruction of a complete directed connectome from a 245 GB anisotropic mouse somatosensory-cortex dataset in 9.7 hours on a single shared-memory CPU system.
ocar.future_work: They present the result as a step toward a microscope-pace streaming connectomics pipeline.

summaries.beginner: To know who talks to whom in brain tissue, you must find the tiny contact points between cells, not just the cell outlines. This paper builds a faster synapse finder by teaching small networks to see membranes, gaps, and packets of messenger chemicals, then combining those clues with simple biological rules.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv report (2017), Santurkar and colleagues detect synapses compositionally from 100 electron-microscopy samples, training lighter networks for membranes, clefts, and vesicles and combining them with rules. They report 7% higher recall and 5% higher F1 than prior state of the art and a 20-fold speed-up. They reconstruct a directed connectome from a 245 GB anisotropic mouse somatosensory-cortex (S1) volume in 9.7 hours on one shared-memory CPU system.
summaries.advanced: Gains are relative to unnamed previous methods in the abstract. The 245 GB S1 volume is anisotropic, which affects appearance of synapses. Completeness of the ‘first complete directed connectome’ from this dataset should be read as a pipeline product on that volume, not a whole-brain mouse map. Training used 100 samples.

plain_language_summary: To know who talks to whom in brain tissue, you must find the tiny contact points between cells, not just the cell outlines. This paper builds a faster synapse finder by teaching small networks to see membranes, gaps, and packets of messenger chemicals, then combining those clues with simple biological rules.

ocar.opportunity: Reconstructing neuronal connectivity requires automated pixel-level segmentation of petabytes of streaming electron-microscopy data. A pipeline that keeps up with multi-beam microscopes would make large-scale connectomics timely.
ocar.challenge: Existing algorithms provide relatively good accuracy but are unacceptably slow and would require years to extract connectivity graphs from even a single cubic millimeter of neural tissue.
ocar.action: Meirovitch and colleagues present a multi-pass pipeline for shared-memory multicore systems: a fast first pass, then a slower pass that iteratively corrects errors, including novel shallow convolutional nets and parallel watershed and merging.
ocar.resolution: They reconstruct the full Kasthuri et al. dataset—463 GB capturing 120,000 cubic microns—from image stack to skeletons in hours on a single multicore machine rather than weeks on larger distributed systems.
ocar.future_work: They demonstrate accuracy of a sparse slow-pass reconstruction and suggest new methods for detecting morphological errors as volumes grow toward a cubic millimeter.

summaries.beginner: Turning a cubic millimeter of brain pictures into a wiring map with today’s slow programs could take years. This paper describes a two-speed pipeline that first traces quickly, then fixes mistakes, fast enough to run on one powerful computer in hours for a published mouse-cortex volume.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv report (2016), Meirovitch and colleagues describe a multi-pass connectomics pipeline for shared-memory multicore machines, aiming at near terabyte-per-hour multi-beam microscope pace. A fast pass is followed by a slower corrective pass using shallow convolutional nets and parallel watershed and merging. They reconstruct the Kasthuri et al. volume (463 GB; 120,000 cubic microns) to skeletons in hours on one machine rather than weeks on larger distributed systems.
summaries.advanced: The abstract contrasts hours versus weeks without naming the prior distributed system. Accuracy is discussed for a sparse slow-pass algorithm rather than as a single overall error rate. The Kasthuri volume is far smaller than the cubic-millimeter scale whose year-scale runtime they warn about.

plain_language_summary: Turning a cubic millimeter of brain pictures into a wiring map with today’s slow programs could take years. This paper describes a two-speed pipeline that first traces quickly, then fixes mistakes, fast enough to run on one powerful computer in hours for a published mouse-cortex volume.

ocar.opportunity: Identifying the exact network of synaptic connections in the fly central nervous system is now a major objective in Drosophila neurobiology, with progress furthest in optic neuropils.
ocar.challenge: Light-microscopic projections of genetically labelled cell types reveal candidates that come into close proximity, but synaptic partnerships are not reliably revealed by such pairs, and unexpected pathways appear in ultrastructure.
ocar.action: Meinertzhagen offers a perspective on Drosophila connectome studies, distinguishing electron-microscopy reconstruction—especially focused-ion-beam milling scanning electron microscopy—from light-microscopic candidate maps, and relating this effort to the C. elegans connectome and vertebrate retina.
ocar.resolution: Synaptic partnerships from ultrastructure provide a heuristic to interpret and predict functional interactions. Circuit analysis can be foiled by degeneracy in pathway elements; circuit motifs and higher-order network properties are additional uses of the maps.
ocar.future_work: Drosophila attempts anticipate parallel work in other systems, notably the inner plexiform layer of vertebrate retina, building on the long-available nematode connectome.

summaries.beginner: Knowing which fly brain cells actually touch, rather than merely pass near each other, is the difference between a guess and a wiring diagram. This perspective explains why electron-microscope maps are needed and how they already help in the fly’s visual system.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neurogenetics (2016), Meinertzhagen reviews Drosophila connectomics, especially optic neuropils and FIB-SEM, and distinguishes those maps from light-microscopic candidate proximity. Ultrastructural synapses often reveal unexpected pathways and support predictions that physiology can test, though degeneracy can foil cell-by-cell causal tests. He places the work alongside the C. elegans connectome and anticipated inner-plexiform reconstructions in vertebrate retina.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a new volume. Dataset tags in the catalog mention C. elegans and mouse retina as comparative context; the essay’s primary subject is Drosophila. Predictive power of anatomy is heuristic, not a substitute for functional tests.

plain_language_summary: Knowing which fly brain cells actually touch, rather than merely pass near each other, is the difference between a guess and a wiring diagram. This perspective explains why electron-microscope maps are needed and how they already help in the fly’s visual system.

ocar.opportunity: Image segmentation typically detects boundaries locally then groups pixels with watershed or connected components. A unified, end-to-end network that directly outputs segments could simplify connectomic reconstruction from volume electron microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Prior pipelines vary the two steps separately, including multi-layer networks for boundaries and global optimizations for clustering, rather than learning segmentation as one process. Object number and size are unknown and highly variable.
ocar.action: Januszewski and colleagues propose flood-filling networks: a recurrent three-dimensional convolutional network that produces individual segments from a raw image, demonstrated on connectomic reconstruction from volume electron microscopy.
ocar.resolution: They report that flood-filling networks substantially improve accuracy over other state-of-the-art methods and can replace complex multi-step pipelines with a single end-to-end network.
ocar.future_work: The approach is offered as a drop-in replacement for multi-step segmentation pipelines on volume electron-microscopy data.

summaries.beginner: Most computer programs first find the edges of objects in a picture and only later decide which pixels belong together. This paper trains one network that grows each object until it is filled, which helps when the number and size of objects are unknown.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv report (2016), Januszewski and colleagues introduce flood-filling networks, a recurrent three-dimensional convolutional model that emits individual segments from raw images. Unlike boundary-then-clustering pipelines, the method is end-to-end trainable and handles unknown, variable object counts and sizes. On volume electron-microscopy connectomic reconstruction they report substantially higher accuracy than other state-of-the-art methods.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not name the electron-microscopy dataset or report numerical error metrics. ‘Substantially improve’ is a qualitative comparison. Recurrent flood-filling still processes objects sequentially, which has engineering implications not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Most computer programs first find the edges of objects in a picture and only later decide which pixels belong together. This paper trains one network that grows each object until it is filled, which helps when the number and size of objects are unknown.

ocar.opportunity: One goal of systems neuroscience is a structure–function model of nervous system organization that would mechanistically link mind, brain, and behavior. A complete connection matrix is a necessary but not sufficient foundation.
ocar.challenge: Connections can be described at nested levels—macroconnections between regions, mesoconnections between neuron types, microconnections between individual neurons, and nanoconnections at synapses—and extracting understanding from vast data is now the greatest challenge.
ocar.action: Swanson and Lichtman review the history of attempts to understand the brain as a system, from fifth-century macro-level ideas through Cajal at the meso- and microlevels to mid-twentieth-century electron microscopy at the nanolevel.
ocar.resolution: They define a connectome as a complete matrix of structural connections between nervous-system nodes and argue that knowledge extraction, not data collection alone, is the present bottleneck.
ocar.future_work: Building structure–function models that use connectomes without treating them as sufficient remains the stated aim.

summaries.beginner: A complete list of who is connected to whom in the nervous system would be a huge help, but it would not by itself explain how the mind works. This review walks through the history of wiring ideas from early anatomy to electron-microscope synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In Annual Review of Neuroscience (2016), Swanson and Lichtman define a connectome as a complete structural connection matrix and distinguish macro-, meso-, micro-, and nano-levels of description. They trace the program from fifth-century regional maps through Cajal to electron microscopy. They argue that a connectome is necessary but not sufficient for a structure–function model, and that extracting understanding from vast data is now the central challenge.
summaries.advanced: This is a historical and conceptual review, not a methods or dataset paper. Nested levels are a taxonomy, not an empirical result. No specific reconstruction metrics are offered.

plain_language_summary: A complete list of who is connected to whom in the nervous system would be a huge help, but it would not by itself explain how the mind works. This review walks through the history of wiring ideas from early anatomy to electron-microscope synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Cellular-resolution connectomics aims at comprehensive connectivity maps from high-throughput nanoscale electron microscopy. Deep learning has shown exceptional image-classification performance and is promising for connectomic analysis.
ocar.challenge: A main challenge is scalable image-analysis algorithms that require minimal user intervention.
ocar.action: Quan, Hildebrand, and Jeong introduce FusionNet, combining semantic segmentation, residual networks, and summation-based skip connections to produce a deeper architecture for automatic segmentation of neuronal structures.
ocar.resolution: They compare performance with several other popular electron-microscopy segmentation methods and illustrate flexibility on cell-membrane and cell-nucleus segmentation.
ocar.future_work: The architecture is positioned for broader connectomic segmentation tasks beyond the two illustrated targets.

summaries.beginner: Finding cell outlines in electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue still takes too much human help. This paper introduces a deep network design meant to label those outlines more accurately with less hand-holding.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers of Computer Science (record year 2016; journal issue 2021), Quan, Hildebrand, and Jeong present FusionNet, a fully residual convolutional network that uses summation skip connections for deeper semantic segmentation. They target automatic labeling of neuronal structures in electron-microscopy connectomics and compare with several popular methods. Flexibility is shown on membrane segmentation and nucleus segmentation.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report numerical scores or dataset names. Journal metadata year (2016) and imprint year (2021) differ; readers should treat bibliographic dating with care. Comparisons are described but not quantified here.

plain_language_summary: Finding cell outlines in electron-microscope pictures of brain tissue still takes too much human help. This paper introduces a deep network design meant to label those outlines more accurately with less hand-holding.

ocar.opportunity: Serial-section electron microscopy can now capture complete specimen volumes up to cubic-millimeter scale, producing multi-terabyte image sets that must be registered before circuits can be traced.
ocar.challenge: Thousands of serial sections must be precisely registered despite rapid variation in biological content and unavoidable data distortions. Phase-only or Pearson correlation can be insufficient as alignment signals.
ocar.action: Wetzel and colleagues introduce SWiFT-IR, which modifies spatial-frequency response during matching to maximize a signal-to-noise alignment measure, and apply it to mouse and zebrafish datasets from Harvard wafer-mapper serial-section electron microscopy.
ocar.resolution: The more robust signal enables iterative registration using projections through multiple sections rather than only adjacent-pair matching, driving alignment into a smooth form that represents complex anatomy such as full-cross-section zebrafish data.
ocar.future_work: The method is developed at the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center for coherent volumetric forms in which neural circuits can be traced and segmented.

summaries.beginner: Brain volumes imaged as thousands of thin slices only become a usable three-dimensional picture after the slices are lined up. This paper describes an alignment method that listens for a cleaner matching signal so warped or changing tissue still registers.
summaries.intermediate: At AIPR (2016), Wetzel and colleagues present SWiFT-IR for registering large serial-section electron-microscopy volumes. Unlike phase-only or Pearson correlation, it adapts spatial-frequency response to maximize a signal-to-noise alignment score. Applied to mouse and zebrafish wafer-mapper datasets, multi-section projection matching plus anatomical constraints in a multi-resolution pyramid produces smooth alignments, including full-cross-section zebrafish data.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report residual alignment error numbers. Mouse and zebrafish examples are named, but dataset identifiers beyond wafer-mapper technology are not given in the text. Success on highly varying anatomy is qualitative (‘smooth form’).

plain_language_summary: Brain volumes imaged as thousands of thin slices only become a usable three-dimensional picture after the slices are lined up. This paper describes an alignment method that listens for a cleaner matching signal so warped or changing tissue still registers.

ocar.opportunity: Reconstructing a connectome from electron-microscopy images currently requires many hours of manual annotation or proofreading. Automatic segmentation is required if cubic-millimeter volumes—about 1 PB of raw data—are to be practical.
ocar.challenge: Manual proofreading does not scale to such volumes.
ocar.action: Knowles-Barley and colleagues update the Rhoana pipeline as RhoanaNet, using deep learning for membrane probability maps and Gala to agglomerate two-dimensional segments into three-dimensional objects, and they apply it to four densely annotated electron-microscopy datasets.
ocar.resolution: Best V_info F-scores were 0.9054 and 0.9182 for two mouse cortex datasets, 0.9438 for lateral geniculate nucleus, and 0.9150 for cerebellum. Source code, training data, test data, and annotations are released at rhoana.org.
ocar.future_work: Public benchmarks are intended to ease comparison and further reduce the proofreading burden.

summaries.beginner: Tracing every cell in a cubic millimeter of brain pictures by hand is not realistic. This paper updates an automatic tracing pipeline, tests it on four mouse-brain electron-microscope volumes, and releases the data so others can compare.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv report (2016), Knowles-Barley and colleagues present RhoanaNet, updating Rhoana with deep-learned membrane maps and Gala agglomeration. They segment four densely annotated volumes: two from mouse cortex plus cerebellum and mouse lateral geniculate nucleus. Best reported V_info F-scores are 0.9054 and 0.9182 for cortex, 0.9438 for LGN, and 0.9150 for cerebellum, with code and data at rhoana.org.
summaries.advanced: F-scores are the best results obtained, not a single default operating point. Two cortex scores are listed without naming which volume is which in the abstract. The 1 PB cubic-millimeter figure is motivational scale, not the size of the four test sets.

plain_language_summary: Tracing every cell in a cubic millimeter of brain pictures by hand is not realistic. This paper updates an automatic tracing pipeline, tests it on four mouse-brain electron-microscope volumes, and releases the data so others can compare.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics has focused on synaptic links, yet extrasynaptic volume transmission via monoamines and neuropeptides is also critical and occurs primarily outside the synaptic connectome.
ocar.challenge: Putative monoamine and neuropeptide connections had not been mapped nervous-system-wide in C. elegans as additional layers alongside synapses and gap junctions.
ocar.action: Bentley and colleagues mapped putative monoamine connections and a subset of neuropeptide connections from new and published gene-expression data and analyzed the resulting multiplex network.
ocar.resolution: The monoamine network is highly disassortative and star-like with a rich-club of broadcasting hubs; the neuropeptide network is more recurrent and clustered. Despite low overlap with the synaptic connectome, significant multilink motifs mark where aminergic and neuropeptide signaling may modulate synapses.
ocar.future_work: The multiplex map is offered as a plan for locating where extrasynaptic signals from a small number of modulatory neurons integrate with wired circuits.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s famous wiring diagram is only the wired part of how its nerve cells communicate; chemicals can also broadcast through tissue. This paper sketches those wireless layers and how they sit on top of the wired map.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS Computational Biology (2016), Bentley and colleagues map putative monoamine connections and a subset of neuropeptide connections in C. elegans from gene-expression data. The monoamine graph is star-like and disassortative with broadcasting rich-club hubs; the neuropeptide graph is more clustered and recurrent. Overlap with the synaptic connectome is low, but multilink motifs suggest sites of modulation. The connectome is treated as synaptic, gap-junction, and neuromodulator layers.
summaries.advanced: Extrasynaptic edges are putative, inferred from expression, not from observing released transmitter. Only a subset of neuropeptide connections is included. Overlap and motif claims are statistical on that inferred graph.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s famous wiring diagram is only the wired part of how its nerve cells communicate; chemicals can also broadcast through tissue. This paper sketches those wireless layers and how they sit on top of the wired map.

ocar.opportunity: Nervous-system maps are critical for understanding development and function. A complete census of cholinergic neuron types would place acetylcholine use in the context of the entire C. elegans connectome.
ocar.challenge: Cholinergic identity across male and hermaphrodite neuron types, including dynamic and sexually dimorphic usage, had not been systematically mapped.
ocar.action: Pereira and colleagues systematically map all cholinergic neuron types in male and hermaphrodite C. elegans and analyze acetylcholine usage relative to other transmitters and network motifs, including expression of acetylcholine-gated anion channels.
ocar.resolution: Acetylcholine is the most broadly used neurotransmitter. They report a sexually dimorphic glutamatergic-to-cholinergic switch in a sex-shared interneuron and suggest acetylcholine may also operate broadly as an inhibitory transmitter. As a first application they identify transcriptional mechanisms controlling cholinergic identity and circuit assembly.
ocar.future_work: The comprehensive neurotransmitter map is positioned for further regulatory and circuit studies.

summaries.beginner: Knowing which worm nerve cells use which chemical messenger is as important as knowing who connects to whom. This paper lists every cell type that uses acetylcholine in both male and hermaphrodite worms.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2015), Pereira and colleagues map all cholinergic neuron types in male and hermaphrodite C. elegans. Acetylcholine is the most broadly used transmitter; they place it in the connectome and in specific network motifs. They describe a sexually dimorphic glutamate-to-acetylcholine switch in a sex-shared interneuron and, from acetylcholine-gated anion-channel expression, suggest acetylcholine may also act inhibitively. They identify transcriptional regulators of cholinergic identity and circuit assembly.
summaries.advanced: Inhibitory acetylcholine is inferred from anion-channel expression patterns, not from direct synaptic physiology in this abstract. ‘Most broadly used’ is a census claim within this map. The dimorphic switch is reported for one sex-shared interneuron class.

plain_language_summary: Knowing which worm nerve cells use which chemical messenger is as important as knowing who connects to whom. This paper lists every cell type that uses acetylcholine in both male and hermaphrodite worms.

ocar.opportunity: Electron microscopy–based connectomics aims to map synaptic connections comprehensively, but current approaches are limited in assigning molecular identities to neurons. Overlaying chemical neuromodulatory maps on synaptic maps would enrich those reconstructions.
ocar.challenge: Standard volume electron microscopy does not directly label molecular identities, especially neuropeptide types.
ocar.action: Shahidi and colleagues use serial multiplex immunogold labeling (siGOLD) with serial-section transmission electron microscopy to identify multiple peptidergic neurons, demonstrating scalability with 11 neuropeptide antibodies on a full-body larval Platynereis ssTEM dataset.
ocar.resolution: High immunogenicity and axonal distribution of neuropeptides allowed identification from small subsets of sections within a larger series. They reconstruct a peptidergic circuit including sensory nuchal organs expressing pigment-dispersing factor, a circadian neuropeptide.
ocar.future_work: The method is offered to overlay neuromodulatory identity onto synaptic connectomes in other nervous systems.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope wiring maps usually cannot tell you which chemical messenger a cell uses. This paper stains thin slices with gold-tagged antibodies so several peptide types can be named inside a full-body map of a worm larva.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2015; bioRxiv record also present), Shahidi and colleagues introduce siGOLD: serial multiplex immunogold labeling on ssTEM. They apply 11 neuropeptide antibodies to a full-body larval Platynereis dataset, identifying neurons from small labeled subsets of a larger series. They reconstruct a circuit in which nuchal organs express pigment-dispersing factor.
summaries.advanced: Molecular IDs come from immunogold on a subset of sections, so unlabeled neurons remain anonymous. Scalability is shown with 11 antibodies on one larval dataset, not an arbitrary antibody panel. Journal metadata list bioRxiv even though the work appeared in eLife.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope wiring maps usually cannot tell you which chemical messenger a cell uses. This paper stains thin slices with gold-tagged antibodies so several peptide types can be named inside a full-body map of a worm larva.

ocar.opportunity: Automating reconstruction of neural circuits from electron-microscopy images needs shared challenges that spur algorithm progress. An international 2D segmentation contest can set a public standard.
ocar.challenge: Creating ground truth is costly, and scoring systems may not be robust. Two-dimensional evaluation has inherent ambiguities and limited test-set size.
ocar.action: Arganda-Carreras and colleagues organized the first international challenge on 2D segmentation of brain electron-microscopy images, scoring submitted boundary maps against a consensus of human expert annotations.
ocar.resolution: The winning team had no prior electron-microscopy experience and used a convolutional network, after which deep learning became accepted as a standard. Cooperation between two teams later produced the best result. Retrospective evaluation showed the scoring system was not robust to variations in neurite-border width; they propose a fix for a future 3D challenge.
ocar.future_work: They conclude the 2D challenge has probably saturated and should be succeeded by a 3D contest with a more robust metric.

summaries.beginner: To push computers to trace cells in brain microscope pictures, researchers held a public contest with a shared test set. A team new to this kind of image won using a deep network, and the contest later revealed that the scoring rules themselves had a flaw.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2015), Arganda-Carreras and a large consortium report the first international 2D electron-microscopy neuron-segmentation challenge. Boundary maps were scored against expert consensus. The winning convolutional-network team had no prior electron-microscopy experience, helping establish deep learning as standard; later cooperating teams did best. The authors say the challenge has probably saturated because of 2D scoring ambiguities and test-set size, and that scores were not robust to neurite-border width.
summaries.advanced: ‘Probably saturated’ is the organizers’ judgment, not a proof that 2D algorithms cannot improve. The proposed scoring fix is for a future 3D challenge, not retroactively applied here. Training-outreach value is explicit: a naive team won.

plain_language_summary: To push computers to trace cells in brain microscope pictures, researchers held a public contest with a shared test set. A team new to this kind of image won using a deep network, and the contest later revealed that the scoring rules themselves had a flaw.

ocar.opportunity: Developmental programs can form neural circuits with similar structure and function among individuals, but how similar entire circuits are across individuals is less well understood.
ocar.challenge: A prior Platynereis larval visual-eye connectome existed for one animal; stereotypy across individuals had not been quantified for the full visual circuit including larval eyespots.
ocar.action: Randel and colleagues acquired a full-body serial-section transmission electron microscopy dataset of another larva of the same age and reconstructed the connectome of the visual eyes and larval eyespots, then compared it anatomically and quantitatively with the earlier map.
ocar.resolution: Comparisons reveal high inter-individual stereotypy of cell complement, neuronal projections, and synaptic connectivity, including left–right asymmetry in some neurons’ connectivity, indicating the larval eye circuitry is hard-wired to that extent.
ocar.future_work: The two-animal comparison sets a template for measuring stereotypy as more Platynereis volumes appear.

summaries.beginner: We often assume animals of the same species are wired the same way, but that is rarely checked cell by cell. This paper maps the visual wiring of a second marine-worm larva and finds it closely matches the first, even down to some left–right differences.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2015), Randel and colleagues reconstruct visual-eye and eyespot circuits from a full-body ssTEM volume of a second Platynereis larva of the same age as a prior reconstruction. Cell complement, projections, and synapses are highly stereotyped between individuals, including left–right connectivity asymmetries in some neurons. They conclude the larval eye circuitry is hard-wired to that extent.
summaries.advanced: Stereotypy is measured between two larvae of one age, not a population. ‘Hard-wired’ is bounded by those two maps. Full-body ssTEM is the substrate; only the visual circuits are compared in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: We often assume animals of the same species are wired the same way, but that is rarely checked cell by cell. This paper maps the visual wiring of a second marine-worm larva and finds it closely matches the first, even down to some left–right differences.

ocar.opportunity: Given an over-segmented electron-microscopy image or volume, accurately clustering regions of the same neuron is central to connectomic reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Existing agglomerative methods do not separately treat superpixels from different biological entities, and merge decisions on newly formed bodies can be premature.
