ocar.action: Parag and colleagues propose a context-aware agglomerative framework that divides superpixels of different biological entities into subsets and agglomerates them separately, plus a delayed scheme that postpones some merge decisions to generate more confident boundary predictions.
ocar.resolution: They report significant improvements in segmentation accuracy over existing standard methods on 2D and 3D datasets.
ocar.future_work: Context-aware delayed agglomeration is positioned as a general clustering stage after over-segmentation.

summaries.beginner: After a computer cuts a microscope picture into too many tiny pieces, it must decide which pieces belong to the same nerve cell. This paper waits on some of those decisions and treats different kinds of tissue pieces separately so it glues more accurately.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS ONE (2014), Parag, Chakraborty, Plaza, and Scheffer introduce context-aware delayed agglomeration for electron-microscopy segmentation. Superpixels from different biological entities are grouped separately, and some merges involving newly formed bodies are postponed for more confident boundaries. They report significant accuracy gains over standard methods on 2D and 3D datasets.
summaries.advanced: ‘Significant improvements’ are not quantified in the abstract, and the 2D and 3D datasets are unnamed. Delayed agglomeration still assumes a useful over-segmentation as input.

plain_language_summary: After a computer cuts a microscope picture into too many tiny pieces, it must decide which pieces belong to the same nerve cell. This paper waits on some of those decisions and treats different kinds of tissue pieces separately so it glues more accurately.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput serial-section electron microscopy now produces massive three-dimensional nanoscale volumes in which neurons and synapses can be observed directly. A fully automated path from images to a brain graph would make those volumes usable.
ocar.challenge: Manual tracing at this scale is unmanageable. State-of-the-art algorithms had focused on particular tasks such as neuron segmentation or synapse identification rather than an end-to-end images-to-graphs pipeline.
ocar.action: Gray Roncal and colleagues present a fully automated images-to-graphs pipeline, define a metric for output-graph quality, search algorithms and parameters for the best operating point, and deploy a reference version on a large public dataset.
ocar.resolution: The reference pipeline provides a baseline and framework for community analysis. All code and data derivatives are made public.
ocar.future_work: The baseline is intended to unlock further algorithm development toward biofidelic computational primitives and understanding of neuropathologies.

summaries.beginner: Huge electron-microscope volumes of brain tissue are only useful if computers can turn them into a list of cells and connections without a person in the loop. This paper describes such an end-to-end pipeline and a way to score the resulting graph.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2014), Gray Roncal and colleagues present what they describe as the first fully automated images-to-graphs pipeline for serial-section electron microscopy, requiring no human interaction. They introduce a metric for output-graph quality and search algorithms and parameters for a best operating point. A reference pipeline is then deployed on a large public dataset, with code and data derivatives released for community baselines.
summaries.advanced: ‘First fully-automated’ is the authors’ claim. The public dataset is not named in the abstract, and no numerical graph-quality scores are given. End-to-end automation still inherits errors from each module (segmentation, synapses, graph construction).

plain_language_summary: Huge electron-microscope volumes of brain tissue are only useful if computers can turn them into a list of cells and connections without a person in the loop. This paper describes such an end-to-end pipeline and a way to score the resulting graph.

ocar.opportunity: Reconstructing circuits at the level of synapses is a central connectomics problem, and electron microscopy is the most proven technique for identifying synapses. Larger datasets make high-throughput annotation essential.
ocar.challenge: Manual synapse identification (proofreading) becomes a major time bottleneck as electron-microscopy datasets grow.
ocar.action: Plaza and colleagues introduce a large-scale, high-throughput, semi-automated methodology to identify synapses and apply it to the Drosophila medulla optic lobe.
ocar.resolution: They annotate many more synapses than previous connectome efforts and argue the approaches are extensible so that synapse identification becomes accessible to a wider community of proofreaders.
ocar.future_work: The medulla application is offered as a template for other large electron-microscopy volumes.

summaries.beginner: Finding every tiny contact between cells in a huge microscope volume by hand would take far too long. This paper describes a semi-automatic way to mark those contacts and uses it in the fruit-fly visual system.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv report (2014), Plaza, Parag, Huang, Olbris, Saunders, and Rivlin present a high-throughput semi-automated synapse-annotation method. Manual identification is the bottleneck as electron-microscopy volumes grow. Applied to the Drosophila medulla optic lobe, they report annotating many more synapses than previous connectome efforts.
summaries.advanced: ‘Many more synapses’ is not quantified in the abstract. The work is semi-automated, so human proofreading remains in the loop. Medulla-specific synapse appearance may not transfer without retraining.

plain_language_summary: Finding every tiny contact between cells in a huge microscope volume by hand would take far too long. This paper describes a semi-automatic way to mark those contacts and uses it in the fruit-fly visual system.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic segmentations of nanometer-scale electron-microscopy volumes require hundreds of corrections per cubic micron, yet humans can split, merge, and adjust segments relatively easily. Better interactive tools could raise throughput.
ocar.challenge: Proofreading is time-consuming, and existing tools needed a quantitative comparison of accuracy, speed, and usability for non-experts.
ocar.action: Haehn and colleagues design Mojo, a single-user desktop proofreading application, and Dojo, a multi-user web application, and run a between-subjects user study in which non-experts proofread neurons in a public connectomics dataset, comparing also to Raveler from Janelia.
ocar.resolution: Web-based Dojo yielded a significant improvement in corrections given the same time, and all Dojo participants reported better usability.
ocar.future_work: They discuss requirements for designing visual proofreading software based on these findings.

summaries.beginner: Computers still need people to fix traced cells in brain microscope volumes, and that work is slow. This paper compares desktop and web tools for those fixes and finds that the web tool helped beginners correct more in the same amount of time.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TVCG (2014), Haehn and colleagues present Mojo (desktop) and Dojo (collaborative web) for proofreading electron-microscopy segmentations that need hundreds of corrections per cubic micron. A between-subjects study asked non-experts to proofread a public connectomics dataset, compared with Raveler. Dojo produced significantly more corrections in a fixed time and better reported usability.
summaries.advanced: The study uses non-experts and a fixed time budget; expert throughput may differ. ‘Hundreds of corrections per cubic micron’ characterizes automatic segmentation burden, not the residual after these tools. Dataset identity is not named in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Computers still need people to fix traced cells in brain microscope volumes, and that work is slow. This paper compares desktop and web tools for those fixes and finds that the web tool helped beginners correct more in the same amount of time.

ocar.opportunity: High-resolution connectomics reconstructs complete neuronal connectivity from electron microscopy by automatic segmentation followed by expert proofreading. Improving the initial segmentation and flagging likely error locations would reduce that burden.
ocar.challenge: Automatic segmentation is error-prone, and experts must still find and fix mistakes.
ocar.action: Nunez-Iglesias and colleagues present gala (graph-based active learning of agglomeration), a Python library that improves agglomerative segmentation and points out image coordinates likely to contain errors, built on the scientific Python stack.
ocar.resolution: They describe software architecture and design choices intended to be useful for other segmentation packages, and they discuss current limitations and how they intend to address them.
ocar.future_work: Planned improvements to the library’s limitations are stated as the next software steps.

summaries.beginner: Automatic tracing of cells in electron-microscope pictures still makes mistakes that experts must hunt down. This paper releases a Python library that both improves how pieces are glued together and marks spots that are likely wrong.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroinformatics (2014), Nunez-Iglesias, Kennedy, Plaza, Chakraborty, and Katz introduce gala, a Python library for graph-based active learning of agglomeration. It aims to improve automatic electron-microscopy segmentation and to highlight likely error coordinates for proofreading. The paper emphasizes architecture on numpy, scipy, networkx, and scikit libraries, plus current limitations.
summaries.advanced: No numerical accuracy gains are reported in the abstract. The work is a library description; ‘improves the state of the art’ is claimed without named baselines here. Active learning still requires some expert labels.

plain_language_summary: Automatic tracing of cells in electron-microscope pictures still makes mistakes that experts must hunt down. This paper releases a Python library that both improves how pieces are glued together and marks spots that are likely wrong.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping networks at synaptic resolution—connectomics—has attracted general interest because automated electron-microscopy collection now makes even large mammalian brains conceivable. Managing the resulting digital information is part of that opportunity.
ocar.challenge: Modern connectomics produces unprecedented quantities of digital data at unprecedented rates and will require breakthrough algorithmic and computational solutions, as genomics did.
ocar.action: Lichtman, Pfister, and Shavit describe key difficulties that may arise for big-data connectomics and provide suggestions for managing them.
ocar.resolution: They frame the problem as a data-intensive computing challenge comparable to early genomics, not only as an imaging or biology problem.
ocar.future_work: The commentary is a call for algorithmic and computational solutions matched to the coming data rates.

summaries.beginner: Mapping every connection in a large brain will create more digital data than biology labs usually handle. This commentary explains why that data flood is a computing problem as much as a microscope problem, similar to the early days of genome sequencing.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2014), Lichtman, Pfister, and Shavit review big-data challenges of connectomics. Automated electron microscopy has extended a program that began with the worm in the 1970s toward large mammalian brains. They argue that unprecedented data volume and rate will require breakthrough algorithms and computing, and they offer management suggestions analogous to genomics.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a system or benchmark. No dataset sizes or throughput numbers are given in the abstract. Suggestions are high-level rather than evaluated implementations.

plain_language_summary: Mapping every connection in a large brain will create more digital data than biology labs usually handle. This commentary explains why that data flood is a computing problem as much as a microscope problem, similar to the early days of genome sequencing.

ocar.opportunity: Recent reconstructions of small but biologically interesting circuits have yielded functional insights from connectomes. Scaling those successes would require a different operational model than heroic manual effort.
ocar.challenge: Those reconstructions required person-months of effort per neuron and will not scale to larger circuits, much less entire animal brains.
ocar.action: Plaza, Scheffer, and Chklovskii examine what generating and using substantially larger connectomes will require.
ocar.resolution: They identify five needs: imaging better suited to automatic reconstruction with excellent z-resolution; automatic synapse detection, validation, and measurement; reconstruction methods that keep uncertainty metrics for every object; fully incremental processes so a connectome can be used before it is complete; and better analysis tools once maps exist.
ocar.future_work: Those five areas are the agenda they set for large-scale reconstruction.

summaries.beginner: Early complete wiring diagrams of small circuits took months of human time per nerve cell, which cannot work for bigger brains. This opinion piece lists five changes—better images, automatic synapse finding, tracking uncertainty, using unfinished maps, and better analysis tools—needed to scale up.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2014), Plaza, Scheffer, and Chklovskii argue that proof-of-concept connectomes will not scale because they cost person-months of effort per neuron. They call for imaging suited to automation with excellent z-resolution, automatic synapse detection and measurement, and uncertainty carried from images through queries. They also want fully incremental use of incomplete maps and better analysis tools once connectomes exist.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/review with no new data. The five-area list is a diagnosis, not an evaluated roadmap. ‘Person-months per neuron’ characterizes then-current heroic reconstructions rather than a measured benchmark here.

plain_language_summary: Early complete wiring diagrams of small circuits took months of human time per nerve cell, which cannot work for bigger brains. This opinion piece lists five changes—better images, automatic synapse finding, tracking uncertainty, using unfinished maps, and better analysis tools—needed to scale up.

ocar.opportunity: Large volumetric electron-microscopy datasets in connectomics need interactive exploration so neuroscientists can pose domain-specific questions on the full-size data.
ocar.challenge: Volumes of several teravoxels, plus segmentation, connectivity, and metadata, are hard to query and visualize concurrently.
ocar.action: Beyer and colleagues present ConnectomeExplorer, combining a knowledge-based query algebra and visual query builder with a scalable volume-visualization framework that handles multiple volumes of several teravoxels each.
ocar.resolution: They evaluate on roughly one terabyte of electron-microscopy data and 750 GB of segmentation, containing over 4,000 segmented structures and 1,000 synapses, and report that collaborators could answer scientific questions on the full-size data for the first time.
ocar.future_work: Query-guided visual analysis is positioned as a way to use connectomic volumes before every biological question is precomputed.

summaries.beginner: A terabyte-scale brain picture is useless if a scientist cannot ask questions of it while looking at the tissue. This paper describes a viewer that lets people build those questions step by step on the full-size volume.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TVCG (2013), Beyer, Al-Awami, Kasthuri, Lichtman, Pfister, and Hadwiger introduce ConnectomeExplorer. A visual query builder composes a knowledge-based query algebra over electron-microscopy, segmentation, connectivity, and metadata volumes at multi-teravoxel scale. Evaluation used about 1 TB of electron-microscopy data and 750 GB of segmentation with over 4,000 structures and 1,000 synapses, enabling collaborators to query full-size data.
summaries.advanced: ‘First time’ is reported from collaborator use-cases, not a controlled study. Structure and synapse counts (over 4,000 and 1,000) describe that evaluation volume. Query power depends on available metadata attributes.

plain_language_summary: A terabyte-scale brain picture is useless if a scientist cannot ask questions of it while looking at the tissue. This paper describes a viewer that lets people build those questions step by step on the full-size volume.

ocar.opportunity: Automated sample preparation and electron microscopy enable very large image datasets. Three-dimensional reconstructions of neuronal processes at nanometer scale can provide new insight into fine-grained brain structure.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation of large-scale electron-microscopy data is the main bottleneck in analysis.
ocar.action: Kaynig and colleagues present a pipeline that trains a random forest on interactive sparse annotations, combines classifier output with an anisotropic smoothing prior in a conditional random field to generate multiple per-image hypotheses, then fuses them into geometrically consistent three-dimensional objects, plus Mojo for proofreading merge errors with sparse scribbles.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate reconstruction from a 27,000 µm^3 volume, a 30 µm cube corresponding to 1,000 consecutive image sections, and provide qualitative and quantitative evaluation.
ocar.future_work: Mojo’s semi-automated merge correction is intended to keep the pipeline usable as volumes grow into the gigabyte–terabyte range.

summaries.beginner: Huge stacks of brain-tissue microscope images still stall when computers must outline every nerve-cell branch. This paper describes a pipeline that learns from a few human marks, builds 3-D cells, and offers a tool to fix accidental mergers.
summaries.intermediate: In Medical Image Analysis (2013), Kaynig and colleagues train a random forest on sparse interactive annotations, generate multiple segmentation hypotheses per image in a conditional random field with an anisotropic smoothing prior, and fuse them into geometrically consistent three-dimensional objects. They reconstruct neuronal processes from a 27,000 µm^3 volume, a 30 µm cube corresponding to 1,000 consecutive sections. They also introduce Mojo, a proofreading tool for semi-automated correction of merge errors from sparse user scribbles.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not report numerical error rates. The 27,000 µm^3 volume is large for the period but far from later millimeter-scale datasets. Random-forest membrane classification predates the later dominance of deep networks.

plain_language_summary: Huge stacks of brain-tissue microscope images still stall when computers must outline every nerve-cell branch. This paper describes a pipeline that learns from a few human marks, builds 3-D cells, and offers a tool to fix accidental mergers.

ocar.opportunity: Opinions diverge on whether mapping synaptic connectivity is worthwhile. If such maps reveal essential circuit characteristics that would otherwise be inaccessible, the effort is justified despite limitations.
ocar.challenge: Critics emphasize limitations of connectomic maps; the field needs an explicit case for what they uniquely provide.
ocar.action: Morgan and Lichtman argue that, albeit their limitations, synaptic connectivity maps will reveal essential characteristics of neural circuits that would otherwise be inaccessible.
ocar.resolution: The commentary takes a position in favor of connectomics as a source of otherwise unavailable circuit knowledge.
ocar.future_work: The argument is a rationale for pursuing maps, not a specific experimental program.

summaries.beginner: Some scientists doubt that listing every brain connection is worth the cost. This short commentary says those maps will still show features of circuits that we cannot get any other way.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2013), Morgan and Lichtman address the debate over whether mapping synaptic connectivity is a good idea. They acknowledge limitations of such maps. They nevertheless argue that wiring diagrams will reveal essential neural-circuit characteristics that would otherwise be inaccessible.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion piece with no data. ‘Essential characteristics’ are not enumerated in the abstract. The piece does not rebut specific technical limitations with new evidence.

plain_language_summary: Some scientists doubt that listing every brain connection is worth the cost. This short commentary says those maps will still show features of circuits that we cannot get any other way.

ocar.opportunity: Some neuroscientists argue that detailed synaptic wiring diagrams will be needed to understand behavior and its disorders. Advances in image acquisition and processing may soon make large-scale circuit reconstruction—connectomics—possible.
ocar.challenge: The community is divided on the feasibility and value of the enterprise.
ocar.action: Lichtman and Sanes revisit objections voiced when the Human Genome Project was proposed, now widely viewed as a success, to ask whether that controversy holds lessons for mapping the connectome.
ocar.resolution: They draw an analogy between early genomics skepticism and contemporary connectomics debate as a way to frame feasibility and value questions.
ocar.future_work: The comparison is meant to inform whether and how to pursue large-scale wiring diagrams.

summaries.beginner: When genome sequencing was first proposed, many people said it was too hard and not worth it; later it was seen as a success. This essay asks whether the same kinds of doubts about mapping brain wiring will look similar in hindsight.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2008), Lichtman and Sanes note division over the feasibility and value of connectomics despite improving image acquisition and processing. They revisit objections to the Human Genome Project as a parallel. The piece asks whether that history holds lessons rather than presenting new reconstructions.
summaries.advanced: Analogies to genomics are rhetorical, not evidence that connectomics will follow the same path. No technical results are reported. Acquisition and graph-analysis stages in the catalog tags reflect the essay’s themes, not a pipeline paper.

plain_language_summary: When genome sequencing was first proposed, many people said it was too hard and not worth it; later it was seen as a success. This essay asks whether the same kinds of doubts about mapping brain wiring will look similar in hindsight.

ocar.opportunity: Community structure in connectomes supports functional specialization, adaptability, and cost-efficient wiring. Nanoscale maps now allow those communities to be studied at the level of individual neurons and synapses.
ocar.challenge: Little was known about communities in connectomes mapped at neuron-and-synapse resolution.
ocar.action: Betzel and colleagues analyze a whole-brain adult Drosophila connectome with a nested stochastic blockmodel to uncover hierarchical community structure, then cluster communities into archetypal meta-clusters from spatial, functional, and molecular properties.
ocar.resolution: Most of roughly 1,500 fine-scale communities are spatially compact, mostly assortative, and aligned with biological features, though nonassortative communities appear in optic lobe and vision pathways. Data-driven clustering grouped communities into 45 archetypical meta-clusters interpreted as modular building blocks of larger, functionally diverse communities.
ocar.future_work: The work highlights statistical network models as tools for interpreting nanoscale connectomes.

summaries.beginner: A whole-brain wiring map can be grouped into neighborhoods of cells that talk among themselves. This preprint finds about fifteen hundred small neighborhoods in the adult fruit fly and then groups those into forty-five reusable building-block types.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026 record), Betzel and colleagues fit a nested stochastic blockmodel to a whole-brain adult Drosophila connectome. Roughly 1,500 finest-scale communities are mostly spatially compact and assortative and match biological features, with nonassortative communities in optic lobe and vision pathways. Clustering on spatial, functional, and molecular properties yields 45 archetypal meta-clusters as candidate functional primitives.
summaries.advanced: Community count (~1500) and 45 meta-clusters are model outputs, not independently labeled cell types. Nonassortative structure is reported as evidence in visual pathways, not as a whole-brain majority. The abstract does not name which adult fly connectome volume was used.

plain_language_summary: A whole-brain wiring map can be grouped into neighborhoods of cells that talk among themselves. This preprint finds about fifteen hundred small neighborhoods in the adult fruit fly and then groups those into forty-five reusable building-block types.

ocar.opportunity: Mossy-fiber connections onto CA3 pyramidal cells are thought to participate in pattern separation, pattern completion, and memory encoding. A large-scale neuronal wiring diagram of those connections would test those ideas anatomically.
ocar.challenge: No large-scale wiring diagram existed for mossy-fiber connections in hippocampal CA3.
ocar.action: Zheng and colleagues assembled a 3D electron-microscopy volume of about 1 × 1 × 0.1 mm^3 from mouse hippocampal CA3, then proofread and automatically segmented all soma-containing neurons and mossy-fiber axons.
ocar.resolution: They classified 1,815 pyramidal cells, 229 inhibitory cells, and over 55,000 mossy-fiber axons, with mossy-fiber input counts rising along a proximodistal gradient and some distal cells showing high convergence through relatively small, vesicle-poor terminals. Shared mossy-fiber inputs exceed degree-preserving random networks and better match proximity-preserving randomization. They also identify a feedforward inhibitory motif from mossy fibers via perisomatic interneurons that selectively target a pyramidal subtype, and share the volume through Pyr.ai.
ocar.future_work: The resource is offered for mapping from circuits to cell types to vesicles in hippocampus.

summaries.beginner: A famous pathway into the hippocampus is thought to help the brain store distinct memories, but its wiring had not been listed at large scale. This paper reconstructs a slab of mouse CA3 and finds a gradient of incoming contacts plus a selective inhibitory detour.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2026), Zheng and colleagues reconstruct an about 1 × 1 × 0.1 mm^3 mouse CA3 volume, classifying 1,815 pyramidal cells, 229 inhibitory cells, and over 55,000 mossy-fiber axons. Mossy-fiber input number increases along a proximodistal gradient, and some distal pyramids receive high convergence through small, vesicle-poor terminals. Shared inputs exceed degree-preserving swaps and resemble proximity-preserving swaps, and a feedforward inhibitory motif via perisomatic interneurons selectively targets a pyramidal subtype; data are on Pyr.ai.
summaries.advanced: The volume thickness is about 0.1 mm, so it is not a complete CA3. Functional roles in pattern separation or completion are motivational, not tested here. ‘Fewer vesicles’ in some small terminals is ultrastructural, not a physiological release measurement.

plain_language_summary: A famous pathway into the hippocampus is thought to help the brain store distinct memories, but its wiring had not been listed at large scale. This paper reconstructs a slab of mouse CA3 and finds a gradient of incoming contacts plus a selective inhibitory detour.

ocar.opportunity: Motif analysis can reveal unique aspects of connectivity in complex networks. The fully reconstructed C. elegans nervous system is an ideal candidate, especially once connection signs are known.
ocar.challenge: Unsigned motif analyses omit excitation versus inhibition; signed motif structure of the worm connectome had not been enumerated with a structure-preserving null model.
ocar.action: Szilágyi and colleagues perform edge-polarity-based signed motif analysis on the C. elegans connectome using recent connection-sign data and a novel structure-preserving randomization method, including a split of nodes by neuron modality.
ocar.resolution: They identify 56 significantly overrepresented and 1 underrepresented three-node signed motifs. Positive feedforward, negative feedback, disinhibitory feedback, and incoherent feedforward loops are overabundant, each with a characteristic neuronal layout by modality.
ocar.future_work: The motif enumeration tool is offered for signed motifs in other complex networks.

summaries.beginner: Once you know not only who connects to whom in the worm but also which links excite or inhibit, you can count small repeating patterns. This paper finds dozens of those signed patterns that show up more often than chance, including loops that feed forward or feed back.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026 record; BMC Biology DOI in metadata), Szilágyi and colleagues run an edge-polarity signed motif analysis of the C. elegans connectome with a structure-preserving random null. They report 56 overrepresented and 1 underrepresented three-node signed motifs, including positive feedforward, negative feedback, disinhibitory feedback, and incoherent feedforward loops. Splitting nodes by neuron modality shows that each significant feedforward or feedback loop has a characteristic neuronal layout.
summaries.advanced: Significance depends on the novel randomization scheme and on the quality of connection-sign assignments. Only three-node motifs are reported. ‘First time’ is the authors’ claim relative to signed, polarity-based analysis.

plain_language_summary: Once you know not only who connects to whom in the worm but also which links excite or inhibit, you can count small repeating patterns. This paper finds dozens of those signed patterns that show up more often than chance, including loops that feed forward or feed back.

ocar.opportunity: Axo-axonic synapses can veto, amplify, or synchronize spikes, but their circuit-scale logic is unknown. A complete adult male Drosophila electron-microscopy connectome makes a census of such synapses onto descending neurons possible.
ocar.challenge: Circuit-scale organization of axo-axonic input onto descending neurons that carry brain commands to the ventral nerve cord had not been charted.
ocar.action: Ceballos and colleagues mapped every axo-axonic input onto 1,314 descending neurons, treating any synapse onto a descending neuron within the cord as axo-axonic by definition, then tested a predicted Giant Fiber motif with immunostaining and optogenetics.
ocar.resolution: They uncovered ascending–descending and interneuron–descending axo-axonic relationships. High-degree neurons integrate without forming an interconnected rich-club. An octet of ascending neurons (AN08B098) provides cholinergic axo-axonic input that increases DNp01 (Giant Fiber) excitability, matching the connectome-derived prediction.
ocar.future_work: The map is offered as a constraint for models of fast motor control.

summaries.beginner: Some contacts land on a nerve cell’s output cable rather than its input branches, which can gate outgoing signals. This paper lists those contacts onto the fly cells that carry commands from brain to body and tests one predicted escape-circuit link.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 iScience/bioRxiv record, Ceballos and colleagues chart all axo-axonic inputs onto 1,314 descending neurons in the adult male Drosophila electron-microscopy connectome, using the definition that cord synapses onto descending neurons are axo-axonic. High-degree cells do not form a rich-club. An AN08B098 octet onto Giant Fibers (DNp01) is cholinergic, and optogenetic activation increases DNp01 excitability.
summaries.advanced: The axo-axonic definition is anatomical (location on descending neurons in the cord), not a physiological veto test for most synapses. Functional validation is reported for one octet–Giant Fiber motif. Catalog dataset tag points at VNC (FANC/MANC) resources used in this space.

plain_language_summary: Some contacts land on a nerve cell’s output cable rather than its input branches, which can gate outgoing signals. This paper lists those contacts onto the fly cells that carry commands from brain to body and tests one predicted escape-circuit link.

ocar.opportunity: Memory engrams form through experience-dependent plasticity of neural circuits, but their detailed synaptic architectures remain unresolved. Nanoscale reconstructions after labeling learning-related ensembles could reveal physical hallmarks of long-term memory.
ocar.challenge: How CA3–CA1 wiring changes among cells recruited during associative learning was unknown at synapse scale.
ocar.action: Uytiepo and colleagues used 3D electron microscopy with chemogenetic labeling of ensembles recruited during associative learning to reconstruct the hippocampal CA3–CA1 pathway.
ocar.resolution: Neurons with a remote history of activity coinciding with memory acquisition showed no strong preference for wiring with each other. Connectomes expanded through multi-synaptic boutons independently of co-activation of postsynaptic partners, with input-specific, spatially restricted synaptic upscaling and remodeling of mitochondria, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, and astrocyte interactions.
ocar.future_work: The structural hallmarks are offered as a basis for cellular flexibility of information coding.

summaries.beginner: Memories are thought to live in changed connections among the cells that were active during learning, but those changes had not been seen in three-dimensional electron-microscope detail. This paper reconstructs a hippocampal pathway after marking those cells and finds more multi-contact endings rather than a simple like-to-like wiring preference.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2025), Uytiepo and colleagues reconstruct mouse hippocampal CA3–CA1 synapses after chemogenetic labeling of ensembles from associative learning. Cells active at memory acquisition did not strongly prefer synapses with each other. Wiring expanded via multi-synaptic boutons regardless of partner co-activation, with local synapse upscaling and organelle and astrocyte remodeling.
summaries.advanced: ‘No strong preference’ is a negative anatomical finding and does not rule out functional like-to-like coding. The labeled ensemble has a remote activity history coinciding with acquisition; acute versus lasting recruitment is not separated in the abstract. Volume electron microscopy here is targeted reconstruction, not a named public millimeter-scale resource.

plain_language_summary: Memories are thought to live in changed connections among the cells that were active during learning, but those changes had not been seen in three-dimensional electron-microscope detail. This paper reconstructs a hippocampal pathway after marking those cells and finds more multi-contact endings rather than a simple like-to-like wiring preference.

ocar.opportunity: A fundamental idea in neuroscience is that cognitive functions are shaped and constrained by structural organization. Linking mapped connectomes to functional predictions remains difficult.
ocar.challenge: Despite progress in mapping structural connectomes, principles linking physical architecture to functional capabilities remain elusive.
ocar.action: Moutuou and Benali introduce an algebraic quantum model in which functional networks emerge as thermal equilibrium (KMS) states of a graph algebra derived from the directed multigraph of C. elegans anatomical and extrasynaptic connectomes.
ocar.resolution: Equilibrium states are used to describe how individual neurons contribute to functional network formation, yielding a functional connectome of topologically driven interactions and an Integration Capacity index for coordinating information flows.
ocar.future_work: The model is offered to connect structural data to functional predictions of cognition and complex behaviors.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram does not automatically tell you how a brain will act. This paper treats the worm’s wired and chemical-broadcast maps as a physical system whose settled states are proposed as stand-ins for function.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 article (journal field empty in the catalog), Moutuou and Benali apply an algebraic quantum / KMS equilibrium framework to C. elegans anatomical and extrasynaptic connectomes. They interpret functional networks as thermal equilibrium states of the graph algebra of the directed multigraph. The model yields a structure-derived functional connectome and an Integration Capacity index that scores how neurons coordinate diverse information flows.
summaries.advanced: The mapping from KMS states to biological function is a modeling interpretation, not a measured neural activity dataset. Journal metadata are incomplete in the catalog row. Extrasynaptic layers inherit uncertainties of those maps.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram does not automatically tell you how a brain will act. This paper treats the worm’s wired and chemical-broadcast maps as a physical system whose settled states are proposed as stand-ins for function.

ocar.opportunity: We can now measure connectivity of every neuron in some neural circuits, but not other biological details such as each neuron’s dynamics. Whether connectivity alone can inform computation is an open question.
ocar.challenge: Single-neuron and single-synapse dynamical parameters are unknown even when a connectome is available.
ocar.action: Lappalainen and colleagues built a model with experimentally determined connectivity for 64 cell types in fruit-fly optic-lobe motion pathways but unknown biophysical parameters, then optimized those parameters with deep-learning methods so the network detects visual motion.
ocar.resolution: Model predictions agreed with experimental measurements of neural activity across 26 studies. They argue the strategy is more likely to succeed when neurons are sparsely connected, a universally observed feature of biological networks.
ocar.future_work: The mechanistic model makes experimentally testable predictions for each neuron in the connectome.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring list still leaves you guessing how strongly each cell and contact behaves in time. This paper fills those unknowns by training a model of the fly’s motion-vision circuit to detect motion, then checks the predicted activity against many published experiments.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2024), Lappalainen and colleagues constrain a network with measured connectivity of 64 cell types in Drosophila optic-lobe motion pathways and optimize unknown single-neuron and synapse parameters so the model detects visual motion. Predictions matched activity measurements across 26 studies. They suggest success is more likely in sparsely connected networks.
summaries.advanced: Agreement with 26 studies is summarized, not broken down in the abstract. Parameters are fitted for motion detection, so other computations could yield different values. Sparse connectivity is invoked as a general biological feature supporting the strategy, not proven here to be sufficient.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring list still leaves you guessing how strongly each cell and contact behaves in time. This paper fills those unknowns by training a model of the fly’s motion-vision circuit to detect motion, then checks the predicted activity against many published experiments.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy can reveal fine structure of neuronal networks but lacks molecular information to identify cell types or functions. Multiplexed labels compatible with electron microscopy would add that overlay.
ocar.challenge: Combining molecular specificity with anatomical ultrastructural context on the same sample has been challenging, especially without detergents that ruin electron-microscopy quality.
ocar.action: Han and colleagues developed fluorescent single-chain variable fragments (scFvs) for multiplexed detergent-free immunolabeling and volumetric correlated light and electron microscopy, generating eight fluorescent scFvs and imaging six probes in female mouse cerebellum by confocal spectral unmixing followed by volume electron microscopy of the same sample.
ocar.resolution: Ultrastructure superimposed with multiple fluorescence channels documented a poorly described cell type, two types of mossy-fiber terminals, and subcellular localization of one ion-channel type. Because scFvs can be derived from existing monoclonal antibodies, hundreds of such probes could be generated.
ocar.future_work: The approach is proposed for molecularly annotated connectomic data.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures show exquisite cell shape but not which molecular tags a cell carries. This paper uses small fluorescent antibody pieces that do not wreck the tissue, so the same cerebellar sample can be colored for several markers and then imaged in the electron microscope.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2024), Han and colleagues introduce detergent-free fluorescent scFv labeling for volumetric CLEM. Eight scFvs targeting brain markers were generated; six were imaged in female mouse cerebellum with spectral confocal microscopy, then the same sample was imaged with volume electron microscopy. They report a poorly described cell type, two mossy-fiber terminal types, and localization of one ion channel, and note that scFvs can be derived from existing monoclonals.
summaries.advanced: Six of eight probes were used in the cerebellum demonstration. ‘Poorly described cell type’ is not named in the abstract. Multiplexing via spectral unmixing still limits how many channels can be separated at once.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures show exquisite cell shape but not which molecular tags a cell carries. This paper uses small fluorescent antibody pieces that do not wreck the tissue, so the same cerebellar sample can be colored for several markers and then imaged in the electron microscope.

ocar.opportunity: When a connectome is available, a student network with the same connectivity but different biophysical parameters can be trained to match a teacher that represents the biological system. Recordings might then remove remaining degeneracy.
ocar.challenge: A connectome is often insufficient to constrain dynamics of networks that perform a specific task, illustrating the difficulty of inferring function from connectivity alone.
ocar.action: Beiran and Litwin-Kumar develop a theory of connectome-constrained recurrent networks in which student and teacher share connectivity but differ in biophysical parameters, and they study when recordings from a subset of neurons identify dynamics.
ocar.resolution: Recordings from a small subset of neurons can remove degeneracy so student dynamics agree with the teacher. The theory can prioritize which neurons to record from to predict unmeasured activity. Solution spaces of connectome-constrained versus unconstrained models are qualitatively different.
ocar.future_work: The framework is offered to determine when connectome-constrained models yield consistent dynamics.

summaries.beginner: Having the same wiring as a real circuit does not guarantee that a model will behave the same way, because each cell’s detailed properties are still unknown. This paper shows theoretically when a few recordings can pin down those unknowns.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2024 bioRxiv record (Nature Neuroscience DOI in metadata), Beiran and Litwin-Kumar analyze student–teacher recurrent networks that share a connectome but not biophysical parameters. Connectivity alone often fails to constrain task dynamics. A small number of recordings can remove degeneracy, and the theory ranks neurons to record to predict the rest. Constrained and unconstrained solution spaces differ qualitatively.
summaries.advanced: This is a theoretical paper; no biological dataset is analyzed in the abstract. ‘Small subset’ is not given as a number. Catalog method tags refer to connectome-constrained visual-system modeling as the topic family, not a fly-vision experiment here.

plain_language_summary: Having the same wiring as a real circuit does not guarantee that a model will behave the same way, because each cell’s detailed properties are still unknown. This paper shows theoretically when a few recordings can pin down those unknowns.

ocar.opportunity: Mapping complete synaptic connectivity of a mammalian brain would reveal pathways underlying perception, behavior, and memory. Serial-section electron microscopy with osmium membrane staining is ideal for visualizing cells and synapses.
ocar.challenge: In whole-brain samples, chemical treatment and volume changes can harm ultrastructure and macroscopic tissue integrity, causing cracks or fragmentation.
ocar.action: Lu and colleagues developed a 12-step protocol, ODeCO, using time-lapse X-ray imaging and brain proxies to infiltrate osmium throughout an entire mouse brain.
ocar.resolution: They report effective osmium infiltration with preserved ultrastructure and without cracks or fragmentation, described as a necessary prerequisite for a comprehensive mouse-brain connectome.
ocar.future_work: The staining strategy is positioned as enabling subsequent serial-section imaging of whole mouse brains.

summaries.beginner: Staining a whole mouse brain for electron microscopy is chemically harsh and can crack the tissue. This preprint describes a twelve-step osmium protocol that, they report, soaks the entire brain without breaking it.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2023), Lu, Wu, Schalek, Meirovitch, Berger, and Lichtman present ODeCO, a 12-step osmium infiltration protocol for whole-mouse-brain serial-section electron microscopy. Time-lapse X-ray imaging and brain proxies guided development. They report preserved ultrastructure without cracks or fragmentation.
summaries.advanced: The abstract does not include electron-microscopy image examples’ quantitative quality scores or a completed whole-brain imaging run. Success is stated for staining integrity, not for a finished connectome. Catalog organism is mouse; no other species is claimed.

plain_language_summary: Staining a whole mouse brain for electron microscopy is chemically harsh and can crack the tissue. This preprint describes a twelve-step osmium protocol that, they report, soaks the entire brain without breaking it.

ocar.opportunity: Visual systems are built from repeating columns, but some genetically and anatomically defined cell types still vary in function. Anatomical connectivity may explain that variability.
ocar.challenge: Tm9 in Drosophila has variable physiological properties despite being a defined cell type across about 800 visual columns.
ocar.action: Cornean and colleagues identified presynaptic inputs of several hundred Tm9 cells across both optic lobes in the FAFB connectome with FlyWire analysis, compared them with more uniform types Tm1 and Tm2, and used genetic synapse labeling plus expansion microscopy across individuals.
ocar.resolution: Tm9 has three major stereotyped inputs and many weaker, sparsely distributed inputs, unlike Tm1 and Tm2, which have one major and more stereotyped input set. Wide-field neurons are a candidate source of variable Tm9 physiology. Heterogeneous wiring exists across individuals.
ocar.future_work: They argue the visual system uses heterogeneous, distributed circuit properties for robust processing.

summaries.beginner: In the fly eye, most cell types behave the same in every column, but one type does not. This paper shows that this type collects a few reliable inputs plus many weaker, scattered ones, which may explain why its responses vary.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2023 bioRxiv record (Nature Communications DOI in metadata), Cornean and colleagues map presynaptic inputs of several hundred Tm9 neurons in FAFB/FlyWire across both optic lobes. Tm9 has three major stereotyped inputs plus many weak sparse inputs, whereas Tm1 and Tm2 have one major, more stereotyped input. Wide-field neurons are proposed as a source of Tm9 variability; expansion-microscopy synapse labeling shows heterogeneous wiring across individuals.
summaries.advanced: ‘Several hundred’ Tm9 cells are mapped, not all ~800 columns. Variable physiology is the motivation; this paper’s new data are anatomical. Expansion microscopy confirms heterogeneity across individuals but is not a full second connectome.

plain_language_summary: In the fly eye, most cell types behave the same in every column, but one type does not. This paper shows that this type collects a few reliable inputs plus many weaker, scattered ones, which may explain why its responses vary.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding molecular anatomy and neural connectivity requires mapping the three-dimensional nanoscale distribution of specific proteins in the context of brain ultrastructure. An all-optical method would be more accessible than correlative light and electron microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy gives molecular specificity and electron microscopy gives ultrastructure, but combining them is challenging.
ocar.action: M’Saad and colleagues present pan-ExM-t: about 24-fold linear expansion of mouse brain samples with fluorescent pan-staining of protein densities for electron-microscopy-like context plus immunolabeling of protein targets.
ocar.resolution: They image synaptic markers Homer1, Bassoon, PSD-95, Synaptophysin, astrocytic GFAP, myelin basic protein, and anti-GFP in neuron cultures and mouse brain sections, revealing those markers in the context of pre- and postsynaptic densities, neuropil nanoarchitecture, and organelles. Lipid labeling visualizes membranes.
ocar.future_work: They highlight potential for high-throughput connectomics studies in any lab with a confocal microscope.

summaries.beginner: Seeing both the identity of a protein and the tiny structure around it usually requires pairing a light microscope with an electron microscope. This paper swells the tissue a great deal, stains proteins generally for context, and still labels chosen molecules—all on a confocal microscope.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2022 bioRxiv record (Nature Biotechnology DOI in metadata), M’Saad and colleagues introduce pan-ExM-t, combining about 24-fold linear expansion with pan-protein-density staining and immunolabeling. Demonstrations in cultures and mouse brain include Homer1, Bassoon, PSD-95, Synaptophysin, GFAP, myelin basic protein, and anti-GFP. Those markers appear in the context of synaptic densities, neuropil nanoarchitecture, and organelles, with lipid labeling for membranes, all on a confocal microscope.
summaries.advanced: Ultrastructural context is expansion-microscopy contrast, not electron microscopy. ~24-fold is linear expansion; volumetric expansion is larger and distortion is not quantified here. ‘High throughput connectomics’ is a stated potential, not a demonstrated whole-circuit map.

plain_language_summary: Seeing both the identity of a protein and the tiny structure around it usually requires pairing a light microscope with an electron microscope. This paper swells the tissue a great deal, stains proteins generally for context, and still labels chosen molecules—all on a confocal microscope.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic segmentation of serial-section electron microscopy is accelerating circuit reconstruction, but accuracy is often limited by the preceding two-dimensional-to-three-dimensional alignment step. Petascale datasets need alignment that is precise and robust to artifacts.
ocar.challenge: Precise, robust alignment in the presence of image artifacts is challenging at petascale, and global optimization can be prohibitively slow.
ocar.action: Popovych and colleagues present a pipeline using self-supervised convolutional nets trained by metric learning to encode and align image pairs, iterative fine-tuning, vector voting against artifacts or missing data, and blockwise distributed alignment composed with decaying transformations instead of a global optimization.
ocar.resolution: Applied to a whole fly-brain dataset, they report improved accuracy relative to prior state of the art, and they demonstrate scaling to a cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex. The pipeline is public as two open-source Python packages.
ocar.future_work: Open-source release is intended to support other petascale serial-section volumes.

summaries.beginner: If successive microscope slices of brain tissue are even slightly misaligned, computers tracing cells will break those cells. This paper describes a large-scale alignment program that works in blocks, votes to ignore bad patches, and was tested on a whole fly brain and a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2022 bioRxiv record (Nature Communications DOI in metadata), Popovych and colleagues align serial-section electron-microscopy images with self-supervised metric-learning networks, vector voting against artifacts, and blockwise transforms with decay instead of a global optimization. They report improved accuracy relative to prior state of the art on a whole fly-brain dataset. They also demonstrate that the pipeline scales to a cubic millimeter of mouse visual cortex and release two open-source Python packages.
summaries.advanced: ‘Improved accuracy’ is not numerically specified in the abstract. Whole fly brain and cubic-millimeter mouse cortex are the two scaling demonstrations; artifact robustness is attributed to vector voting without a reported failure-rate table here.

plain_language_summary: If successive microscope slices of brain tissue are even slightly misaligned, computers tracing cells will break those cells. This paper describes a large-scale alignment program that works in blocks, votes to ignore bad patches, and was tested on a whole fly brain and a cubic millimeter of mouse cortex.

ocar.opportunity: Posterior parietal cortex exhibits choice-selective activity during perceptual decision-making, but how that selectivity arises from synaptic connectivity was unknown.
ocar.challenge: Relating synapses between neurons to their selective activity requires combining behavior, physiology, electron microscopy, and modeling.
ocar.action: Kuan and colleagues combined virtual-reality behavior, two-photon calcium imaging, high-throughput electron microscopy, and circuit modeling to analyze how synaptic connectivity among posterior parietal neurons relates to selective activity.
ocar.resolution: Excitatory pyramidal neurons preferentially target inhibitory interneurons with the same selectivity; those interneurons preferentially target pyramids of opposite selectivity, forming an opponent-inhibition motif. Circuit models indicate that motif amplifies selective inputs, induces competition between opposite-selectivity populations, and improves encoding of trial-type information.
ocar.future_work: The results are offered as evidence for how cortical synaptic connectivity supports a learned decision-making task.

summaries.beginner: When an animal makes a choice, some brain cells become active for one option and not the other, but it was unclear how their connections produce that split. This paper pairs living-activity measurements with an electron-microscope wiring map of the same cortical area and finds a push–pull inhibitory pattern.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2022 bioRxiv record (Nature DOI in metadata), Kuan and colleagues combine virtual-reality decisions, two-photon imaging, electron microscopy, and modeling in posterior parietal cortex. Pyramids prefer inhibitory partners of the same choice selectivity; those interneurons prefer pyramids of opposite selectivity (opponent inhibition). Models say the motif amplifies selectivity and improves trial-type encoding.
summaries.advanced: Organism is not named in the abstract (catalog organism list is empty). Opponent inhibition is reported for the reconstructed and imaged population, not as a universal cortical rule. Model benefits for encoding are computational, not a causal lesion test in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: When an animal makes a choice, some brain cells become active for one option and not the other, but it was unclear how their connections produce that split. This paper pairs living-activity measurements with an electron-microscope wiring map of the same cortical area and finds a push–pull inhibitory pattern.

ocar.opportunity: Deep learning has improved three-dimensional neuron segmentation, but errors remain in regions with image defects. Point-cloud methods might merge neuron fragments across gaps of missing sections.
ocar.challenge: A common defect is consecutive missing image sections, which split neuron segmentations across the gap. Prior methods have not attempted large gaps with an efficient representation.
ocar.action: Berman, Chklovskii, and Wu treat merging as classification on point-cloud representations of neurons and train CurveNet to identify which fragments should be merged.
ocar.resolution: They report strong performance that scales to gaps well beyond prior methods, with high performance at data volumes that would be unfeasible for other methods, suggesting point clouds for other proofreading tasks.
ocar.future_work: They see point-cloud representations as viable for additional proofreading problems beyond missing-section merges.

summaries.beginner: When a few microscope slices are missing, a traced nerve cell can look like two broken pieces. This paper turns those pieces into sparse point clouds and trains a network to decide which pieces should be rejoined, even across large gaps.
summaries.intermediate: At MIDL (2021), Berman, Chklovskii, and Wu classify whether neuron fragments should merge using CurveNet on point-cloud representations, targeting splits from consecutive missing sections. They report strong performance that scales to gaps well beyond prior methods. Point clouds remain data-efficient at sizes that would be unfeasible for other representations, suggesting use in further proofreading tasks.
summaries.advanced: No numerical accuracy or gap-size figures appear in the abstract. The task is framed as classification of merge candidates, so candidate generation is a separate problem. Claims versus ‘other methods’ are not named here.

plain_language_summary: When a few microscope slices are missing, a traced nerve cell can look like two broken pieces. This paper turns those pieces into sparse point clouds and trains a network to decide which pieces should be rejoined, even across large gaps.

ocar.opportunity: Invertebrate muscle cells often connect through desmosomes anchored by intermediate filaments. Mapping those adhesive networks alongside synapses would show how force and motor commands spread through a body.
ocar.challenge: Desmosomal networks had not been reconstructed for all somatic muscles in an entire larva.
ocar.action: Jasek and colleagues skeletonized 853 muscle cells and their desmosomal partners in volume electron microscopy covering an entire Platynereis larva, then mapped motoneuron synapses onto that desmosomal connectome.
ocar.resolution: Muscle cells adhere to each other and to epithelial, glial, ciliated, and bristle-producing cells and basal lamina, forming a desmosomal connectome of over 2,000 cells. Aciculae are highly connected hubs, matching many degrees of freedom of movement in video microscopy. Motoneuron synapses on the map infer the tissue extent influenced by each motoneuron.
ocar.future_work: Cellular-level maps of synaptic and adherent-force networks are offered to elucidate body mechanics.

summaries.beginner: Muscles are not only driven by nerve contacts; they also stick to other cells and to a supporting sheet, which spreads force. This paper maps those sticky junctions for every body muscle in a marine-worm larva and links them to motor-nerve contacts.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2021), Jasek and colleagues skeletonize 853 muscle cells and desmosomal partners in a whole Platynereis larva volume-EM dataset, yielding a desmosomal connectome of over 2,000 cells. Aciculae emerge as hubs, consistent with video-microscopy degrees of freedom. Overlaying motoneuron synapses estimates tissue influenced by each motoneuron.
summaries.advanced: Desmosomal ‘connectome’ edges are adhesive junctions, not chemical synapses. Hub status of aciculae is anatomical plus behavioral correlation, not a causal mechanics experiment. Whole-larva coverage is claimed for this volume.

plain_language_summary: Muscles are not only driven by nerve contacts; they also stick to other cells and to a supporting sheet, which spreads force. This paper maps those sticky junctions for every body muscle in a marine-worm larva and links them to motor-nerve contacts.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has a stereotyped complement of neurons connected in a consistent manner, and transparency allows visualization of identified neurons in living animals. Those properties make it advantageous for structure–function studies of the nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Methods for structure, connectivity, synapses, and activity are evolving rapidly, so practitioners need an up-to-date methods account.
ocar.action: Emmons, Yemini, and Zimmer describe methods for studying C. elegans nervous-system structure and function, including fluorescent neuron identification, electron-microscopy connectomics, fluorescent synapse sensors, and calcium reporters for single-neuron and system-wide activity.
ocar.resolution: They highlight enhanced neuron-specific reporter use, new more powerful electron-microscopy techniques, verification of electron-microscopy reconstructions with fluorescent synapse probes, and advances that open observation of activity across the nervous system.
ocar.future_work: Recommended methods are intended to encourage new C. elegans work as connectomic techniques continue to expand.

summaries.beginner: The roundworm is unusually convenient for brain research because every nerve cell can be named and watched in a living, see-through animal. This methods review explains current ways to see those cells’ shapes, connections, and activity.
summaries.intermediate: In Genetics (2021), Emmons, Yemini, and Zimmer review methods for C. elegans neuronal structure and activity. Transparency and a stereotyped nervous system support fluorescent identification, electron-microscopy connectomics, synapse-level fluorescent probes, and calcium imaging from single cells to the whole nervous system. They emphasize newly efficient reporter strategies and up-to-date electron-microscopy recommendations.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods review, not a new connectome. Recommendations will date as techniques change. Catalog tags include electron microscopy and the White-style C. elegans dataset as the field context.

plain_language_summary: The roundworm is unusually convenient for brain research because every nerve cell can be named and watched in a living, see-through animal. This methods review explains current ways to see those cells’ shapes, connections, and activity.

ocar.opportunity: Credit assignment is a key problem in learning; biological systems lack a plausible mechanism equivalent to backpropagation. A synaptic architecture that implements a node-perturbation variant of reinforcement learning would be evidence for a local solution.
ocar.challenge: How vertebrate basal ganglia could assign credit at the synaptic level was not established anatomically.
ocar.action: Kornfeld and colleagues used automated connectomic analysis of two volume electron-microscopy datasets of songbird Area X to test predictions of a reinforcement-learning model, then built a biophysical model from the electron-microscopy data.
ocar.resolution: Axons encoding exploratory variability terminate predominantly on dendritic shafts, while axons encoding song timing (context) terminate predominantly on spines, matching model predictions. The biophysical model suggests that this synaptic dichotomy facilitates efficient learning.
ocar.future_work: The findings are presented as evidence for a general, biologically plausible credit-assignment model in vertebrate basal ganglia.

summaries.beginner: When a bird practices a song, the brain must decide which tiny connection changes helped. This paper shows that in a songbird learning area, exploration-related inputs and timing-related inputs land on different parts of the same cells, matching a proposed local learning rule.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Kornfeld, Januszewski, Schubert, Jain, Denk, and Fee reconstruct songbird basal ganglia (Area X) from two volume electron-microscopy datasets. Variability-encoding axons prefer dendritic shafts and context/timing axons prefer spines, as a node-perturbation reinforcement-learning model predicted. A biophysical model based on the data suggests the dichotomy aids efficient learning.
summaries.advanced: Predictions tested are anatomical termination preferences, not in vivo credit-assignment dynamics. Two vEM datasets of Area X are used; generality to other basal ganglia is an inference. Backpropagation is discussed as implausible in biology, not empirically disproven here.

plain_language_summary: When a bird practices a song, the brain must decide which tiny connection changes helped. This paper shows that in a songbird learning area, exploration-related inputs and timing-related inputs land on different parts of the same cells, matching a proposed local learning rule.

ocar.opportunity: Nervous systems are built from a deep repertoire of neuron types, but gene-expression programs that specify individual neuron identities are poorly understood. A profile matching C. elegans anatomy and wiring at single-cell resolution would close that gap.
ocar.challenge: An expression profile of all 302 C. elegans neurons matched to the wiring diagram had not been produced.
ocar.action: Taylor and colleagues produced that nervous-system-wide expression catalog and used computational approaches to find cis-regulatory elements and candidate adhesion proteins for synaptic specificity and process placement.
ocar.resolution: Individual neuron classes appear identifiable by combinatorial expression of specific gene families; each class expresses unique codes of about 23 neuropeptide genes and about 36 neuropeptide receptors, pointing to an expansive wireless signaling network. Data are at cengen.org and CengenApp.
ocar.future_work: The directory is expected to spur studies of anatomy, connectivity, and function throughout the C. elegans nervous system.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s 302 nerve cells are each genetically distinct, but the full gene recipe for every cell was missing. This paper provides that recipe and finds that combinations of messenger genes could identify each cell class.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Taylor and colleagues profile gene expression in all 302 C. elegans neurons at single-cell resolution matched to anatomy and the wiring diagram. Neuron classes appear identifiable by combinatorial gene-family codes, including about 23 neuropeptide genes and about 36 neuropeptide receptors per class. They computationally identify cis-regulatory elements and candidate adhesion proteins, with data at cengen.org and CengenApp.
summaries.advanced: Neuropeptide and receptor counts are approximate (~23 and ~36) combinatorial codes, not proof of functional release at those numbers of partners. Adhesion and cis-regulatory findings are computational predictions. The catalog is expression, not a new electron-microscopy connectome.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s 302 nerve cells are each genetically distinct, but the full gene recipe for every cell was missing. This paper provides that recipe and finds that combinations of messenger genes could identify each cell class.

ocar.opportunity: Large three-dimensional electron-microscopy reconstructions encompass thousands of neurons and millions of synapses. Automatically classifying fragments as axon, dendrite, or soma would support analysis and proofreading.
ocar.challenge: Interpreting reconstructions at this scale demands automated morphology analysis, including subcompartment identity and merge-error detection.
ocar.action: Li, Januszewski, Jain, and Li use three-dimensional convolutional networks on full voxel input to classify reconstructed neuron fragments as axon, dendrite, or soma, then use localized predictions to detect and correct merge errors.
ocar.resolution: They achieve a mean F1-score of 0.972, exceeding the previous state of the art of 0.955, and detect 90.6% of inter-class merge errors with a 2.7% false-positive rate.
ocar.future_work: Predictions are positioned to support multiple analysis and proofreading applications.

summaries.beginner: Once a computer has traced pieces of nerve cells, it still needs to know whether a piece is an output cable, an input branch, or the cell body. This paper trains a three-dimensional network to label those parts and to catch cases where two different cells were glued together.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2020), Li, Januszewski, Jain, and Li classify volume electron-microscopy neuron fragments as axon, dendrite, or soma with 3D convolutional networks on voxels. They report a mean F1-score of 0.972, exceeding a previous state of the art of 0.955. Finely localized labels detect 90.6% of inter-class merge errors at a 2.7% false-positive rate.
summaries.advanced: Merge-error detection is for inter-class errors (e.g., axon glued to dendrite), not all merge errors. F1 0.972 is a mean; class-wise scores are not given. Dataset names are omitted in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Once a computer has traced pieces of nerve cells, it still needs to know whether a piece is an output cable, an input branch, or the cell body. This paper trains a three-dimensional network to label those parts and to catch cases where two different cells were glued together.

ocar.opportunity: Large electron-microscopy connectomics datasets comprise thousands to millions of overlapping two-dimensional tiles that must be registered into a coherent volume. An efficient solver for matching features would unlock joint alignment of very large series.
ocar.challenge: Existing solvers are inadequate for large volumes and inefficient for small-scale registration. Reliable priors for regularization may be absent.
ocar.action: Khairy, Denisov, and Saalfeld present a matrix-based solver that minimizes feature-pair squared distances with explicit regularization, constructing a rigid-model approximation as prior when needed, and delegate the linear system to available computer programs.
ocar.resolution: The method jointly aligned 2.67 million images with more than 200 million point-pairs and was used to align the first full adult fruit-fly brain.
ocar.future_work: Scale-up is delegated to the linear-system solvers whose performance they briefly compare.

summaries.beginner: A fly-brain electron-microscope dataset is millions of overlapping snapshots that must be stitched into one volume. This paper solves that alignment as a large math problem and reports lining up millions of images for the first complete adult fruit-fly brain.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv report (2018), Khairy, Denisov, and Saalfeld formulate joint deformable registration of electron-microscopy tiles as a regularized linear system, using a rigid-model prior when biological priors are lacking. Existing solvers, they argue, were inadequate for large volumes and inefficient at small scale. They jointly aligned 2.67 million images with more than 200 million point-pairs and used the method to align the first full adult fruit-fly brain.
summaries.advanced: Alignment success is not accompanied by residual-error statistics in the abstract. ‘First full adult fruit fly brain’ refers to alignment of that series, not proofread connectivity. Solver comparison is described as brief.

plain_language_summary: A fly-brain electron-microscope dataset is millions of overlapping snapshots that must be stitched into one volume. This paper solves that alignment as a large math problem and reports lining up millions of images for the first complete adult fruit-fly brain.

ocar.opportunity: The electrical synapse pattern of a nervous system is defined by neuron-type-specific innexin complements. Mapping innexin expression nervous-system-wide would describe that electrical connectome and its plasticity.
ocar.challenge: How innexin expression, and thus electrical synapses, change when C. elegans enters the dauer arrest stage was not known at nervous-system scale.
ocar.action: Bhattacharya and colleagues systematically analyze expression of the 14 neuronally expressed innexins, then focus on remodeling of 12 of them in dauer, and relate changes to locomotion and chemosensory behavior with genetic analysis of individual electrical synapses and an intersectional gene-regulatory mechanism.
ocar.resolution: Innexin expression is a highly complex combinatorial pattern that changes in a neuron-type-specific manner in dauer for 12 of 14 neuronal innexins. Dauer-specific electrical-synapse remodeling accounts for aspects of altered locomotion and chemosensation. Terminal selector and FoxO transcription factors induce innexin changes in a neuron-type- and environment-specific manner.
ocar.future_work: The work illustrates nervous-system-wide dynamics of electrical synapses and regulatory strategies that produce them.

summaries.beginner: Besides chemical contacts, worm nerve cells are linked by electrical pores whose recipe of building-block proteins differs by cell type. This paper shows that when the worm enters a hardy resting stage, those recipes change in many cells, helping to explain altered movement and smell behavior.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2018), Bhattacharya, Aghayeva, Berghoff, and Hobert map innexin expression across the C. elegans nervous system. Combinatorial patterns are complex; 12 of 14 neuronal innexins change in a neuron-type-specific way in dauer. Remodeling of specific electrical synapses contributes to dauer locomotion and chemosensation. Terminal selectors and FoxO factors implement the changes intersectionally.
summaries.advanced: Electrical synapses are inferred from innexin expression and selected genetic tests, not a full electron-microscopy gap-junction census in dauer. Two of 14 neuronal innexins are not described as changing. Behavior links are demonstrated for several individual synapses, not every expression change.

plain_language_summary: Besides chemical contacts, worm nerve cells are linked by electrical pores whose recipe of building-block proteins differs by cell type. This paper shows that when the worm enters a hardy resting stage, those recipes change in many cells, helping to explain altered movement and smell behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Deep learning has begun to impact neuroscience, including claims of super-human accuracy in connectomic segmentation. A challenge that favors generalization across sources and tissues would make those tools usable beyond the training domain.
ocar.challenge: Current algorithms do not effectively generalize beyond the particular source and brain tissues used for training, limiting usability. The authors show state-of-the-art methods perform poorly on a new challenge.
ocar.action: Linsley and colleagues describe the STAR challenge for source- and tissue-agnostic neuron reconstruction and introduce a convolutional recurrent module combining short-range horizontal connections and long-range top-down connections between stages.
ocar.resolution: The architecture establishes state of the art on STAR and is presented as a step toward widely usable, fully automated connectomics analysis.
ocar.future_work: Broad generalization, not dataset-specific fitting, is the stated goal for subsequent segmentation systems.

summaries.beginner: Computer programs that trace nerve cells can look superhuman on the pictures they were trained on and then fail on a different microscope or brain region. This paper proposes a harder contest that mixes sources and tissues and a network designed to do better there.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv report (2018), Linsley, Kim, Berson, and Serre introduce STAR, a source- and tissue-agnostic neuron-reconstruction challenge, after showing that leading methods fail to generalize beyond their training tissue. They propose a convolutional recurrent module with intra-stage horizontal and inter-stage top-down connections. That architecture establishes state of the art on STAR as a step toward more widely usable automated connectomics.
summaries.advanced: STAR performance numbers are not in the abstract. ‘Super-human’ refers to prior claims the authors contest for generalization, not a metric they reproduce here. The new module’s gains are challenge-specific.

plain_language_summary: Computer programs that trace nerve cells can look superhuman on the pictures they were trained on and then fail on a different microscope or brain region. This paper proposes a harder contest that mixes sources and tissues and a network designed to do better there.

ocar.opportunity: Humans detect merge errors by acquiring intuition for correct neuronal morphology. Teaching three-dimensional convolutional networks to use high-level shape could catch merges that local classifiers miss.
ocar.challenge: Deep-learning connectomics algorithms rely on localized classification rather than overall morphology, producing many erroneously merged objects. Biological neurons have complicated, variable shapes, and merge errors take many forms.
ocar.action: Rolnick and colleagues present MergeNet, showing that 3D ConvNets can detect merge errors from high-level morphology, with unsupervised training that operates across datasets, tested on connectomics data and on merged MNIST images.
ocar.resolution: They demonstrate MergeNet performance on a variety of connectomics data and on a merged-MNIST dataset created as a controlled morphology test.
ocar.future_work: Cross-dataset unsupervised merge detection is offered as a morphology-aware complement to local voxel classifiers.

summaries.beginner: Computers that label pixels in brain pictures often glue two cells into one because they never look at the overall shape. This paper trains a network to notice when a traced object has an impossible shape, using a method that does not need extra human-drawn answers.
summaries.intermediate: In an arXiv report (2017), Rolnick and colleagues introduce MergeNet, a 3D convolutional net for detecting merge errors from neuronal morphology. Training is unsupervised and intended to operate across datasets. They test on connectomics volumes and on merged MNIST digits as a shape-control dataset.
summaries.advanced: No detection-rate numbers appear in the abstract. Unsupervised training still requires a definition of merged versus unmerged objects in the procedure (not specified here). MNIST is an analogy, not neural tissue.
