plain_language_summary: Computers that label pixels in brain pictures often glue two cells into one because they never look at the overall shape. This paper trains a network to notice when a traced object has an impossible shape, using a method that does not need extra human-drawn answers.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic electron-microscopy volumes, often hundreds of terabytes, must be segmented to identify cell boundaries, synapses, and organelles. Tracking the state of that long, multi-tool, multi-user process would support management and auditing.
ocar.challenge: Segmentation of a single volume is complex, time-intensive, and performed with a diverse set of tools and many users, creating provenance and accountability problems.
ocar.action: Al-Awami and colleagues present NeuroBlocks, a multi-user web application that integrates manual and semi-automatic segmentation, proofreading, visualization, and analysis tools and visually tracks the evolution of large volumetric segmentations.
ocar.resolution: They describe a design based on domain-task analysis and demonstrate utility with two case studies of different user roles in a large real-world connectomics project.
ocar.future_work: The system is positioned as the first to integrate this heterogeneous tool set for provenance and auditing of large-scale segmentations.

summaries.beginner: A huge brain-image project uses many programs and many people over a long time, so it is easy to lose track of what has been fixed. This paper presents a shared website that shows the history and status of tracing and checking work.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TVCG (2016), Al-Awami and colleagues introduce NeuroBlocks, a web system for tracking segmentation and proofreading of hundred-terabyte-scale electron-microscopy volumes. It integrates diverse manual and semi-automatic tools and records provenance. Two case studies address different user roles on a large real-world project.
summaries.advanced: ‘First system’ is the authors’ integration claim. Case studies are qualitative utility demonstrations, not controlled error-rate experiments. Volume size ‘hundreds of terabytes’ describes the domain, not necessarily the case-study subset.

plain_language_summary: A huge brain-image project uses many programs and many people over a long time, so it is easy to lose track of what has been fixed. This paper presents a shared website that shows the history and status of tracing and checking work.

ocar.opportunity: Resurgent interest in synaptic circuitry and plasticity has emphasized three-dimensional reconstruction from serial-section electron microscopy. Public, densely reconstructed hippocampal volumes would support training, modeling, and tool development.
ocar.challenge: Densely reconstructed hippocampal neuropil volumes with original images and traces had not been freely available as a community resource.
ocar.action: Harris and colleagues imaged three volumes of adult rat hippocampal CA1 neuropil at about 2 nm X–Y resolution on serial sections about 50–60 nm thick and densely reconstructed all axons, dendrites, glia, and synapses in a cube, a cylinder, and a parallelepiped of increasing size.
ocar.resolution: Volumes are about 10 µm^3 around a large spine, about 43 µm^3 around a 3.4 µm oblique dendrite, and about 178 µm^3 around a 4.9 µm apical dendrite. They provide ultrastructural standards, reconstructions for biophysical modeling, and a test bed for tools, with data at the Open Connectome Project.
ocar.future_work: The resource is intended for user training and reconstruction-tool development.

summaries.beginner: Researchers need shared, carefully traced examples of hippocampal tissue so people and programs can learn what synapses look like from every angle. This paper releases three small but fully traced pieces of adult rat CA1.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Data (2015), Harris and colleagues densely reconstruct three adult rat CA1 neuropil volumes from serial-section electron microscopy at about 2 nm in X–Y and 50–60 nm section thickness: about 10, 43, and 178 µm^3 around a spine, an oblique dendrite (3.4 µm), and an apical dendrite (4.9 µm). All axons, dendrites, glia, and synapses are reconstructed; a subset of dendrites includes microtubules, polyribosomes, smooth endoplasmic reticulum, and endosomes. Data are at the Open Connectome Project.
summaries.advanced: These are local neuropil samples, not a hippocampal connectome. Anisotropic section thickness (50–60 nm) versus 2 nm in plane limits z-resolution. Catalog organism tag is ‘other’ (rat).

plain_language_summary: Researchers need shared, carefully traced examples of hippocampal tissue so people and programs can learn what synapses look like from every angle. This paper releases three small but fully traced pieces of adult rat CA1.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput brain imaging, initially three-dimensional electron-microscopy stacks, needs a scalable database cluster for spatial analysis and annotation to build connectomes with parallel computer-vision algorithms.
ocar.challenge: Workloads that build neural connectivity maps require partitioning space, avoiding read/write I/O interference, and simple scalable programming interfaces.
ocar.action: Burns and colleagues describe the Open Connectome Project data cluster: spatial-index partitioning across nodes, reads to parallel disk arrays and writes to solid-state storage, and RESTful Web services, publicly at openconnecto.me.
ocar.resolution: They include a production-system performance evaluation highlighting spatial data organization. The design inherits from NoSQL scale-out and data-intensive architectures.
ocar.future_work: The public services and open-science datasets are intended to support connectome-building pipelines more broadly.

summaries.beginner: Computer-vision programs that trace brain images need a database that can store and fetch three-dimensional neighborhoods quickly. This paper describes a cluster built for that job and opened to the public.
summaries.intermediate: At SSDBM (2013), Burns and colleagues present the Open Connectome Project data cluster for spatial analysis and annotation of high-throughput imaging, starting with 3D electron microscopy. Data are partitioned by spatial index; reads and writes go to different storage tiers; interfaces are stateless REST. They report production performance emphasizing spatial organization, with services at openconnecto.me.
summaries.advanced: Performance numbers are not in the abstract. The system is designed for connectome workloads but is infrastructure, not a completed wiring diagram. Time-series and multi-channel data are mentioned as additional targets.

plain_language_summary: Computer-vision programs that trace brain images need a database that can store and fetch three-dimensional neighborhoods quickly. This paper describes a cluster built for that job and opened to the public.

ocar.opportunity: How different local cortical circuitry is from a random network can be tested with dense physiological sampling of connections among identified cells. Nonrandom features would constrain models of cortical computation.
ocar.challenge: The fine-scale statistical structure of synaptic connectivity among layer 5 pyramidal neurons was incompletely known.
ocar.action: Song and colleagues probed connections with several hundred simultaneous quadruple whole-cell recordings from layer 5 pyramidal neurons in rat visual cortex and analyzed motif frequencies and synaptic strengths.
ocar.resolution: Bidirectional connections are more common than in a random network, and several clustered three-neuron patterns are overrepresented. Connection strength follows a lognormal rather than Poisson distribution, concentrating weight in a few synapses, and strengths sharing a pre- or postsynaptic neuron are correlated. The local network is described as a skeleton of stronger connections in a sea of weaker ones.
ocar.future_work: They argue that skeleton should be investigated further for its role in network dynamics.

summaries.beginner: If cortical cells connected at random, two-way links and tight triangles would be rare, and most contacts would be similarly weak. This paper’s four-cell recordings in rat visual cortex show extra two-way links, extra clusters, and a few much stronger synapses.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS Biology (2005), Song, Sjöström, Reigl, Nelson, and Chklovskii made several hundred quadruple whole-cell recordings from rat visual-cortex layer 5 pyramids. Bidirectional connections and some three-neuron motifs exceed random expectation. Amplitude distributions fit lognormal better than Poisson, concentrating strength, and shared-cell strengths correlate, yielding a strong-connection skeleton among weaker links.
summaries.advanced: This is paired recording, not electron-microscopy connectomics; catalog stage tags include proofreading in a broad sense of circuit curation. ‘Several hundred’ recordings are not given as an exact N. Lognormal fits describe amplitudes in this preparation, not all cortical layers.

plain_language_summary: If cortical cells connected at random, two-way links and tight triangles would be rare, and most contacts would be similarly weak. This paper’s four-cell recordings in rat visual cortex show extra two-way links, extra clusters, and a few much stronger synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Dense electron-microscopy connectomes map neuronal structure and wiring at synaptic resolution. Scalable representations that integrate structure and connectivity with minimal human labels would support discovery in those maps.
ocar.challenge: Learning representations that combine morphology and connectivity for connectome discovery with little intervention remains difficult. Coarse skeletons may discard identity information.
ocar.action: Shi and colleagues present a self-supervised hierarchical graph neural network with skeleton decomposition for contrastive learning on finely sampled FlyWire neuronal skeletons, then build structure-driven connectivity representations and iterative multi-hop learning.
ocar.resolution: Fine skeletons preserve substantially richer identity information than coarse ones; coordinate-free topology reduces developmental and geometric confounds. Structure-driven connectivity improves subtype discrimination without predefined partner-type labels. Multi-hop learning reveals hemispheric lateralization and connectivity-defined subgroups, with attention pointing to specific synaptic partners.
ocar.future_work: The framework is offered for discovering neuronal identity and organization in large dense connectomes.

summaries.beginner: A whole-brain fly map contains so many cells that grouping them still usually needs expert labels. This preprint trains a model on cell shape and then on who connects to whom, so similar cells cluster with little human naming.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Shi, Chen, Liu, and Zhang learn self-supervised structure–connectivity representations from finely sampled FlyWire skeletons using a hierarchical graph net. Fine skeletons beat coarse ones for identity; coordinate-free topology reduces geometric confounds. Embedding synaptic partners improves subtype discrimination without partner-type labels; multi-hop learning finds hemispheric lateralization and connectivity-defined subgroups.
summaries.advanced: Improvements are described qualitatively (‘substantially richer,’ ‘improving’) without numerical scores in the abstract. FlyWire is the dense connectome used; transfer to other volumes is not shown. Attention-based partner explanations are model interpretations.

plain_language_summary: A whole-brain fly map contains so many cells that grouping them still usually needs expert labels. This preprint trains a model on cell shape and then on who connects to whom, so similar cells cluster with little human naming.

ocar.opportunity: Neurodevelopment is complex yet robust; the C. elegans brain connectome across post-embryonic life is a tractable place to ask how network cores form. The worm brain has on the order of 200 neurons yet diverse behaviors.
ocar.challenge: How core organization and hub structure of the worm brain change after hatching, while edge density increases, was not described in these network terms.
ocar.action: Yadav and Singh study the developing C. elegans brain connectome through the post-embryonic phase, examining edge density, core persistence, rich-club structure, and in-degree k-core centralization.
ocar.resolution: Starting with most head neurons present at hatching, the brain adds many synapses and increases edge density while remaining weakly connected, which they interpret as balancing communication and hierarchy. The core mixes a conserved backbone of persistent neurons with transient or recurring cells, and a rich club present from an early stage selectively strengthens. Input hubs are preserved and the in-degree k-core becomes more centralized, consistent with previously reported asymmetric synapse addition.
ocar.future_work: They present the results as a perspective on neurodevelopment that may facilitate understanding of function.

summaries.beginner: Even a tiny worm brain keeps adding connections after birth. This preprint watches that growing network and finds a stable inner group of cells plus a rich-club of well-connected cells that tightens over time.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Yadav and Singh analyze post-embryonic development of the C. elegans brain connectome. Edge density rises from added synapses while overall connectivity stays weak. A core mixes persistent neurons with transient or recurring ones; a rich club is present early and strengthens. Input hubs persist and in-degree k-cores centralize, in line with known asymmetric synapse addition.
summaries.advanced: ‘Around 200 neurons’ refers to the brain subset, not the entire 302-neuron nervous system. Developmental conclusions depend on which staged connectomes are used (not named in the abstract). Functional interpretation of weak connectivity as balancing communication and hierarchy is inferential.

plain_language_summary: Even a tiny worm brain keeps adding connections after birth. This preprint watches that growing network and finds a stable inner group of cells plus a rich-club of well-connected cells that tightens over time.

ocar.opportunity: After volume electron-microscopy acquisition, assembling millions of images into a coherent three-dimensional volume is the first critical reconstruction step. Robust montaging and alignment without heavy deep learning or extensive hand edits would widen access.
ocar.challenge: Existing methods work best on artifact-free datasets or rely on computationally intensive deep learning or time-consuming human editing, restricting broader use of volume electron microscopy.
ocar.action: Wu and Lichtman developed FEABAS, a scalable open-source package that elastically montages and aligns electron-microscopy datasets using adaptive mesh modeling and finite-element methods.
ocar.resolution: FEABAS is described as handling common artifacts such as wrinkles, folds, tears, and broken sections while remaining lightweight across computational environments.
ocar.future_work: The tool is intended to underpin downstream analyses on imperfect but typical volume electron-microscopy acquisitions.

summaries.beginner: Real electron-microscope series of brain tissue often have wrinkles, tears, or missing bits that break naive stitching. This preprint releases an alignment program that treats the images as a stretchable mesh so those defects are less fatal.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2026), Wu and Lichtman introduce FEABAS for elastic montaging and alignment of serial electron-microscopy data via adaptive meshes and finite elements. Existing methods, they argue, work best on artifact-free data or else need heavy deep learning or extensive hand edits. FEABAS is designed to handle wrinkles, folds, tears, and broken sections while remaining lightweight across computational environments.
summaries.advanced: No quantitative alignment-error comparisons appear in the abstract. ‘Lightweight’ is a design claim across environments, not a benchmarked runtime. Success on artifacts is described as robust handling rather than a measured residual.

plain_language_summary: Real electron-microscope series of brain tissue often have wrinkles, tears, or missing bits that break naive stitching. This preprint releases an alignment program that treats the images as a stretchable mesh so those defects are less fatal.

ocar.opportunity: Volume electron microscopy provides nanometer-scale three-dimensional imaging, but axial resolution is often much lower than in-plane resolution. Isotropic reconstruction would help segmentation and connectomic reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: Anisotropic volumes hinder segmentation and reconstruction; interpolation and prior learning-based methods can hallucinate textures or drift between slices.
ocar.action: Qiu and colleagues present a two-stage cross-axial super-resolution framework: DINOv3-style self-distillation of a vision transformer on high-resolution xy sections, then a conditional diffusion denoiser trained on simulated z-downsampling with a frozen-ViT perceptual loss.
ocar.resolution: On two public volume electron-microscopy datasets they report improved fidelity, perceptual quality, and membrane-boundary continuity over interpolation and learning-based baselines, with reduced hallucinated textures and inter-slice drift.
ocar.future_work: The method is aimed at making anisotropic acquisitions more usable for connectomics.

summaries.beginner: Many three-dimensional electron-microscope volumes are sharp sideways but blurry up and down, which makes tracing membranes harder. This paper trains a generative model, guided by a vision transformer, to invent the missing in-between detail more consistently.
summaries.intermediate: In Electronics (2026), Qiu and colleagues combine DINOv3-style vision-transformer pretraining on high-resolution xy volume electron-microscopy sections with a conditional diffusion model trained on simulated z-downsampling. A frozen-ViT perceptual loss is meant to keep generated slices statistically close to real sections. On two public datasets they report better fidelity, perceptual quality, and membrane continuity than interpolation and prior learning methods, with less hallucination and slice drift.
summaries.advanced: Supervision uses simulated z-downsampling, which may not match real axial blur and missing wedges. Generative super-resolution can still invent non-physical textures even if reduced. Dataset names are not given. Catalog stages include segmentation and modeling because the output is intended to aid those steps.

plain_language_summary: Many three-dimensional electron-microscope volumes are sharp sideways but blurry up and down, which makes tracing membranes harder. This paper trains a generative model, guided by a vision transformer, to invent the missing in-between detail more consistently.

ocar.opportunity: Brain function requires plasticity at multiple scales, and neuroimaging shows large-scale functional network remodeling in development and after injury. Electron-microscopy connectomes and single-cell projectomes now reveal axonal structural complexity that might support that remodeling without growing entirely new long-distance axons.
ocar.challenge: How large-scale network remodeling is achieved microscopically is unknown, because growth of entirely new long-distance axons is unlikely.
ocar.action: Richards, Huang, Bauer, and Lee review evidence from electron-microscopic connectomes and single-cell projectomes across model organisms on arborized axons, differentially myelinated branches, and axonal regions devoid of synapses that could form new contacts.
ocar.resolution: They consider whether these conserved axonal features could enable long-range functional plasticity, particularly after focal brain injury, contributing to an emerging view of large-scale adaptive reorganization.
ocar.future_work: The review frames these ultrastructural features as candidate substrates for network-level repair and plasticity.

summaries.beginner: After injury or during growth, large-scale brain networks can change even if new long cables probably do not grow across the brain. This review asks whether the already-complex branches of existing axons—some even lacking contacts today—could form new connections later.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2026), Richards, Huang, Bauer, and Lee argue that large-scale functional remodeling seen in neuroimaging cannot rely on growing wholly new long-distance axons. Electron-microscopy connectomes and projectomes show highly arborized axons, branch-specific myelination, and synapse-free axonal stretches that could later synapse. They propose these conserved features as substrates for long-range plasticity after focal injury.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; no new volume is presented. The link from synapse-free axon stretches to future synaptogenesis is a hypothesis. Electron microscopy is a source of evidence, not a methods contribution here.

plain_language_summary: After injury or during growth, large-scale brain networks can change even if new long cables probably do not grow across the brain. This review asks whether the already-complex branches of existing axons—some even lacking contacts today—could form new connections later.

ocar.opportunity: Many animals have mechanosensory neurons that fire when a limb nears its physical range, but the function of those proprioceptive limit detectors is poorly understood. Identified hair plates on the Drosophila leg plus a connectome make causal tests possible.
ocar.challenge: The behavioral role of specific hair-plate proprioceptors, and whether each is specialized for reflexes matched to the joint limit it detects, was unclear.
ocar.action: Pratt and colleagues combine calcium imaging in behaving flies, reconstruction of CxHP8 axons in an electron-microscopy dataset, optogenetic activation and silencing, and comprehensive reconstruction of other hair plates’ morphology and downstream connectivity.
ocar.resolution: A coxal hair plate (CxHP8) detects limits of anterior leg movement and is wired to excite posterior and inhibit anterior movement. Activation elicited posterior postural reflexes; silencing altered the swing-to-stance transition during walking. Other hair plates are predicted to control reflexes matched to the joint limits they detect.
ocar.future_work: The work illustrates predicting sensorimotor reflexes from a connectome with identified proprioceptive inputs and motor outputs.

summaries.beginner: Some sensors fire when a limb is about to go too far, like a mechanical stop. This paper shows that one such sensor on the fruit-fly leg both feels the front-most position and is wired to push the leg back, and that turning it off changes walking.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2026), Pratt and colleagues study Drosophila leg hair plates. Calcium imaging shows coxal CxHP8 detects anterior movement limits. Electron-microscopy reconstruction indicates it excites posterior and inhibits anterior motor pathways. Optogenetic activation drives posterior postural reflexes; silencing alters swing-to-stance transitions. Other hair plates’ predicted functions follow from peripheral morphology and downstream connectivity.
summaries.advanced: Direct physiology plus connectome is reported for CxHP8; other hair plates are predictions from reconstruction. Walking effects of silencing are described as altered transitions, not a full kinematic table in the abstract. Catalog method is electron microscopy.

plain_language_summary: Some sensors fire when a limb is about to go too far, like a mechanical stop. This paper shows that one such sensor on the fruit-fly leg both feels the front-most position and is wired to push the leg back, and that turning it off changes walking.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila early olfactory system is a leading model for olfactory processing and associative memory, now with dense electron-microscopy connectomes of every cell type, neuron, and synapse along the pathway.
ocar.challenge: A wiring diagram, however complete, does not by itself reveal functional logic. Reviews of the past fifteen years of connectome and synaptome data still leave feedback-loop abstractions under-specified.
ocar.action: Lazar and Zhou review early-olfactory-system connectome and synaptome datasets, emphasizing that the feedforward pathway is embedded in dense local feedback among large-scale multi-input multi-output neurons, and they argue for explicit models of natural odorant objects and causal, real-time cascade dynamics.
ocar.resolution: They propose that systematic understanding of feedback-loop abstractions at each neuropil stage is the foundation of functional logic, together with odorant semantics/syntax and new distance measures for classifying odorant objects in support of associative memory.
ocar.future_work: They call for quantitative models that treat the circuit as a real-time cascade of giant local feedback loops constrained by natural odor statistics.

summaries.beginner: Having a complete parts-and-wires list of the fly’s early smell pathway is not the same as knowing how it computes. This essay argues that dense local feedback, not just the famous feedforward chain, plus a model of real-world odors, is what we still need.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 article (journal field empty), Lazar and Zhou review fifteen years of Drosophila early-olfactory connectome and synaptome data. They stress that feedforward paths sit inside large multi-input multi-output local feedback circuits. Functional logic, they argue, requires abstractions of those loops, an explicit model of natural odorant objects, and causal real-time analysis of stage-by-stage feedback.
summaries.advanced: This is a conceptual review, not a new reconstruction. Catalog method is electron microscopy as the data source under discussion. No new counts or experiments are reported.

plain_language_summary: Having a complete parts-and-wires list of the fly’s early smell pathway is not the same as knowing how it computes. This essay argues that dense local feedback, not just the famous feedforward chain, plus a model of real-world odors, is what we still need.

ocar.opportunity: Neural communication uses both fast synaptic transmission and slower extrasynaptic signaling, but how the two jointly organize function is unclear. Complete synaptic and neuropeptidergic connectomes of C. elegans allow a unified multiplex comparison.
ocar.challenge: Linking anatomical wiring to functional communication across synaptic and extrasynaptic layers lacked a single framework.
ocar.action: Sunil, Benali, and Moutuou infer structure-derived functional connectivity from the synaptic connectome using statistical-physics equilibrium principles and compare that layer with the extrasynaptic connectome.
ocar.resolution: They describe four regimes: a topology-dependent layer reinforcing synaptic motor circuits; a topology-resilient modulatory layer for global regulation and behavioral state; a purely extrasynaptic network for survival and homeostasis; and a purely synaptic regime for rapid sensorimotor processing.
ocar.future_work: The strategy is offered as a general way to integrate structural and modulatory connectomes.

summaries.beginner: Worms communicate both through wired contacts and through slower chemical broadcasts, and it has been unclear how those two systems share the work. This paper compares a physics-inspired map of likely synaptic information flow with the peptide broadcast map and finds four different styles of communication.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 article (journal field empty), Sunil, Benali, and Moutuou build a multiplex picture of C. elegans synaptic and neuropeptidergic connectomes. Equilibrium statistical-physics inference yields a probabilistic functional layer from synaptic wiring, compared with extrasynaptic maps. They parse four regimes spanning topology-dependent motor reinforcement, resilient modulation, purely extrasynaptic homeostasis, and purely synaptic low-latency sensorimotor processing.
summaries.advanced: Functional connectivity is inferred from equilibrium assumptions, not measured activity. Four-regime labels are interpretive. Journal metadata are missing in the catalog. Results inherit uncertainties of the neuropeptidergic map.

plain_language_summary: Worms communicate both through wired contacts and through slower chemical broadcasts, and it has been unclear how those two systems share the work. This paper compares a physics-inspired map of likely synaptic information flow with the peptide broadcast map and finds four different styles of communication.

ocar.opportunity: Comprehensive mapping of neural connections is essential for understanding brain function, but automated reconstructions still require extensive manual correction. An AI system that evaluates plausible assemblies of fragments could raise proofreading throughput.
ocar.challenge: Existing automated methods introduce errors that require time-consuming manual correction, a critical bottleneck, especially for axons in large volumes.
ocar.action: Januszewski and colleagues developed PATHFINDER, which segments volumetric data, proposes ways to assemble neuron fragments, and evaluates the plausibility of resulting shapes, applied to all axons in an IBEAM-mSEM mouse-cortex volume.
ocar.resolution: They report that PATHFINDER reduces axon-reconstruction error rate by an order of magnitude over previous state of the art, implying proofreading throughput improvements of up to 84× relative to prior estimates in a whole-mouse-brain context.
ocar.future_work: By reducing manual effort, the advance is positioned to unlock both large-scale connectome mapping and routine analysis of smaller volumes.

summaries.beginner: Computers still break axons into pieces that people must stitch, which is the slow step in mapping brains. This preprint describes a system that guesses how pieces fit by checking whether the resulting shape looks like a real neuron, and it reports far fewer leftover mistakes.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2025), Januszewski, Templier, Hayworth, Peale, and Hess introduce PATHFINDER for assembling axon fragments from volumetric segmentation using shape-plausibility scoring. On all axons in an IBEAM-mSEM mouse-cortex volume they report an order-of-magnitude lower axon error rate than prior state of the art. They translate that gain into proofreading throughput improvements of up to 84× relative to prior estimates in a whole-mouse-brain context.
summaries.advanced: The 84× figure is relative to prior estimates in a whole-mouse-brain context, not a measured whole-brain run. ‘Order of magnitude’ error reduction is not given as an exact rate in the abstract. Results are for axons in one IBEAM-mSEM cortex volume.

plain_language_summary: Computers still break axons into pieces that people must stitch, which is the slow step in mapping brains. This preprint describes a system that guesses how pieces fit by checking whether the resulting shape looks like a real neuron, and it reports far fewer leftover mistakes.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding how circuit connectivity relates to function is crucial for uncovering how the brain computes. In mouse primary visual cortex, excitatory neurons with similar responses are more likely to connect, but broader rules across layers and areas were unknown.
ocar.challenge: Whether like-to-like connectivity extends across layers, areas, and feedback connections, and whether feature versus spatial tuning predicts synapses beyond axon–dendrite proximity, was open.
ocar.action: Ding and colleagues leverage the millimetre-scale MICrONS dataset to analyze synaptic connectivity and functional properties across cortical layers and areas, using a digital twin to split feature versus spatial tuning, and they train recurrent networks on a classification task for comparison.
ocar.resolution: Neurons with similar responses are preferentially connected within and across layers and areas, including feedback, supporting like-to-like connectivity across the visual hierarchy. Only the feature component of a digital-twin split, not spatial receptive-field location, predicts fine-scale synapses beyond axon–dendrite proximity, and postsynaptic cohorts are more similar than a pairwise like-to-like rule predicts. Recurrent networks trained on a classification task develop similar pairwise and higher-order rules, and ablating like-to-like connections impairs performance more than ablating random connections.
ocar.future_work: These principles are suggested to play a role in sensory processing and learning, highlighting shared structure with artificial systems.

summaries.beginner: Cells that respond to similar visual patterns tend to connect in mouse visual cortex, but it was unclear how far that rule goes. This paper uses a millimetre-scale map plus recorded activity and finds the rule holds across layers and areas, driven by what cells prefer, not just where their receptive fields sit.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2025), Ding and colleagues analyze MICrONS mouse visual cortex connectivity and function. Like-to-like connectivity appears within and across layers and areas, including feedback. A digital twin splits feature versus spatial tuning; only features predict fine-scale synapses beyond axon–dendrite proximity. Higher-order similarity of postsynaptic cohorts exceeds pairwise like-to-like. Classification-trained recurrent nets develop similar rules, and ablating like-to-like weights hurts more than random ablation.
summaries.advanced: Universality is claimed for the visual hierarchy in this dataset, not all cortex. Digital-twin validation is mentioned as ‘validated’ without metrics here. Artificial-network ablation is a model experiment, not a biological lesion.

plain_language_summary: Cells that respond to similar visual patterns tend to connect in mouse visual cortex, but it was unclear how far that rule goes. This paper uses a millimetre-scale map plus recorded activity and finds the rule holds across layers and areas, driven by what cells prefer, not just where their receptive fields sit.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian neocortex contains diverse cell types mapped by molecular, electrophysiological, and morphological methods. Cellular-scale electron microscopy adds unbiased ultrastructure, synapses, and nanometre-scale morphology for tens of thousands of neurons, most incompletely reconstructed.
ocar.challenge: Identifying cell types in such volumes is a clear analysis challenge when most cells lack complete arbors.
ocar.action: Elabbady and colleagues systematically survey the somatic region of all cells in a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex using quantitative electron-microscopy features.
ocar.resolution: The perisomatic region is sufficient to identify cell types, including types defined primarily by connectivity. Classification facilitates cell-type-specific connectivity characterization and locating cells with rare connectivity patterns.
ocar.future_work: Perisomatic ultrastructure is offered as a practical classifier for incomplete reconstructions in millimeter-scale volumes.

summaries.beginner: In a cubic millimetre of cortex, most cells are only partly traced, so you cannot always use the whole shape to name the cell type. This paper shows that measurements around the cell body in electron-microscope data are enough to classify types, even types known mainly by their connection patterns.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2025; 2024 DOI tail in metadata), Elabbady and colleagues quantify perisomatic ultrastructure for all cells in a cubic millimetre of mouse cortex (MICrONS). They argue that the somatic region is sufficient to identify cell types even when most arbors are incomplete. Classification includes types defined primarily by connectivity and helps locate cells with rare wiring patterns.
summaries.advanced: Sufficiency of perisomatic features is demonstrated in this volume; transfer to other regions or species is not shown. Most neurons remain incomplete reconstructions, so type labels are local-ultrastructure inferences. Catalog year 2025 versus DOI 2024-07765 should be checked against the publisher record.

plain_language_summary: In a cubic millimetre of cortex, most cells are only partly traced, so you cannot always use the whole shape to name the cell type. This paper shows that measurements around the cell body in electron-microscope data are enough to classify types, even types known mainly by their connection patterns.

ocar.opportunity: Researchers have long noted differences in synapse counts between electron-microscopy reconstructions of similar Drosophila circuitry. Isolating the contribution of sample preparation and imaging technique would clarify those discrepancies.
ocar.challenge: Confounds include sample-size differences, software detection efficiency, and proofreading dependence, mixing true biological variation with technical visibility.
ocar.action: Scheffer compares raw synapse counts across major Drosophila reconstructions—FANC, MANC, FAFB (original and new synapses), male CNS, BANC, and hemibrain, plus smaller volumes—compensating where possible for size and software detection, to estimate synapses visible to a skilled human, using regions reconstructed in common for each pair.
ocar.resolution: In almost all known cases reconstructed by both techniques, isotropic FIB-SEM shows more human-visible synapses than microtome-sliced reconstructions, typically by more than 40%. This strongly suggests, but does not conclusively prove, that synapses are easier to see in isotropic FIB-SEM data.
ocar.future_work: The comparison is framed as an efficiency estimate per compartment and for whole samples, to interpret count differences across community volumes.

summaries.beginner: Different fly wiring maps disagree on how many contacts they see, which might be biology or just the microscope method. This preprint compares many reconstructions and finds that the even-resolution ion-beam method usually shows more contacts than sliced transmission images, by more than forty percent in matched regions.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2025), Scheffer compares raw, proofreading-independent synapse counts across FANC, MANC, FAFB (two synapse versions), male CNS, BANC, hemibrain, and smaller Drosophila volumes, adjusting for sample size and software detection. Matched regions show isotropic FIB-SEM reconstructions with typically more than 40% more human-visible synapses than microtome ssTEM-style volumes. He treats this as strong but not conclusive evidence that synapses are easier to see in FIB-SEM.
summaries.advanced: The conclusion is explicitly not proof of a biological difference. ‘Typically by more than 40%’ is a summary across pairs, not every pair. Human-visible estimates still depend on residual confounds the author tries to compensate for.

This preprint compares many reconstructions and finds that the even-resolution ion-beam method usually shows more contacts than sliced transmission images, by more than forty percent in matched regions.

ocar.opportunity: Split-GAL4 driver lines allow specific targeting of cell types in Drosophila, enabling functional, transcriptomic, and proteomic studies. Linking those lines to electron-microscopy connectomes would let anatomy and genetics meet.
ocar.challenge: A large, validated, curated collection spanning adult central nervous system and larval cell types, screened for specificity, had not been released as a single resource.
ocar.action: Meissner and colleagues describe collections of 3,060 lines targeting adult Drosophila central-nervous-system cell types and 1,373 lines characterized in third-instar larvae, resulting from screening over 77,000 split hemidriver combinations, with images related to electron-microscopy connectomes via NeuronBridge and other tools.
ocar.resolution: Lines are validated for driver expression and curated for cell-type specificity. They also make available 300,000 new 3D images of other split-GAL4 lines, plus fly stocks.
ocar.future_work: The resource is intended for precise anatomical targeting aligned to connectomes.

summaries.beginner: To turn a fly cell type on or off, researchers need genetic switches that hit just those cells. This preprint releases thousands of such switches for adult and larval nervous systems and ties their light-microscope pictures to electron-microscope wiring maps.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2024), Meissner and colleagues report 3,060 adult central-nervous-system split-GAL4 lines and 1,373 third-instar larval lines, from over 77,000 hemidriver combinations, curated for specificity. NeuronBridge links light-microscopy images to electron-microscopy connectomes. An additional 300,000 3D images of other split-GAL4 lines are released with stocks.
summaries.advanced: Specificity is curated, not claimed to be absolute for every line. Catalog method tag is electron microscopy because of the connectome link, not because this paper is an electron-microscopy methods paper. Larval and adult collections are separate counts.

plain_language_summary: To turn a fly cell type on or off, researchers need genetic switches that hit just those cells. This preprint releases thousands of such switches for adult and larval nervous systems and ties their light-microscope pictures to electron-microscope wiring maps.

ocar.opportunity: Cell density and spatial distribution within tissue inform physiology. X-ray holographic nanotomography can resolve subcellular details in millimetre-scale volumes relevant to neuronal circuits, but nuclei must be found automatically.
ocar.challenge: Datasets covering about mm^3 make manual annotation of individual nuclei unrealistic.
ocar.action: Nathansen and colleagues developed and trained an automated classifier that detects and segments cell nuclei in mouse brain tissue imaged with x-ray holographic nanotomography, using a high-performance cluster and browser-compatible outputs for multi-user proofreading.
ocar.resolution: The system provides locations and morphologies of about 80,000 nuclei per dataset with high recall and generalizes to similar biological-replicate datasets with minimal additional ground truth.
ocar.future_work: The classifier is offered for integration into automated histological pipelines for synchrotron x-ray holographic nanotomography in systems neuroscience and broader tissue studies.

summaries.beginner: A millimetre-scale X-ray scan of mouse brain contains tens of thousands of cell nuclei that no one can mark by hand. This paper trains a computer to find those nuclei and packages the results so several people can check them in a browser.
summaries.intermediate: At SPIE Optical Engineering + Applications (2024), Nathansen and colleagues segment nuclei in mouse-brain x-ray holographic nanotomography volumes of about mm^3. The classifier reports about 80,000 nuclei per dataset with high recall and transfers to biological replicates with little extra ground truth. Outputs are tables plus browser-viewable segmentations and meshes for proofreading.
summaries.advanced: ‘High recall’ is not given as a percentage. Catalog dataset tag includes MICrONS, indicating mouse-cortex context in the collection, though the abstract describes XNH mouse brain generally. Proofreading remains in the workflow.

plain_language_summary: A millimetre-scale X-ray scan of mouse brain contains tens of thousands of cell nuclei that no one can mark by hand. This paper trains a computer to find those nuclei and packages the results so several people can check them in a browser.

ocar.opportunity: Updated chemical and gap-junction connectomes of both adult C. elegans sexes, including muscle, enable a fuller reading of circuits and of neurons that remained unstudied. Network-wide analyses can suggest functions for those cells.
ocar.challenge: Despite decades of research, circuits underlying behavior remain incompletely described and functions of many neurons are still unknown.
ocar.action: Emmons analyzes the updated whole-animal connectomes with modularity, degree, and pathway-convergence measures, emphasizing body-wall muscle as an end organ and previously unrecognized neuron groups.
ocar.resolution: Modularity divides the graph into 10 communities correlated with broad behavior categories, with body-wall muscle acting both as a major information sink and as a sensory source in a feedback loop. Most interneurons have similar in- and out-degrees, so they disperse information as much as they aggregate it. The analysis also highlights high-degree ventral-cord interneurons linked by many gap junctions, a body-wide mechanosensory field onto two interneurons, and additional circuits involving unstudied neurons.
ocar.future_work: Insights are offered to guide theory and experiments on individual neurons, groups, and circuits.

summaries.beginner: Even in the worm, whose wiring has been studied for decades, many cells still have no known job. This paper re-reads the updated whole-animal maps and points to new groupings, including a possible processing chain in the ventral cord and a body-wide touch field.
summaries.intermediate: In PLOS Biology (2024), Emmons analyzes updated adult male and hermaphrodite C. elegans chemical and gap-junction connectomes including muscle. Ten modules match broad behavioral categories. Body-wall muscle is both a convergence sink and a sensory source. Interneurons often disperse as much as they aggregate. High-degree gap-junction-linked ventral-cord interneurons and a two-interneuron mechanosensory field covering the body are highlighted, along with circuits involving unstudied neurons.
summaries.advanced: Community–behavior correlations are interpretive. Suggested functions of unstudied neurons are hypotheses from anatomy, not new activity data. Completeness depends on the updated connectome releases used.

plain_language_summary: Even in the worm, whose wiring has been studied for decades, many cells still have no known job. This paper re-reads the updated whole-animal maps and points to new groupings, including a possible processing chain in the ventral cord and a body-wide touch field.

ocar.opportunity: Neurons express various neurotransmitter-receptor subunit combinations and receive inputs from cells using different transmitters. Localizing receptor subtypes to specific synaptic inputs would molecularly characterize synapses in a connectome.
ocar.challenge: Assigning receptor subunits to particular incoming connections has been difficult.
ocar.action: Sanfilippo and colleagues use epitope-tagged endogenous receptor subunits, expansion light-sheet microscopy, and electron-microscopy connectomics in Drosophila, focusing on directionally selective motion-sensitive neurons, and genetically test a transmembrane protein found at a spatially restricted synapse class.
ocar.resolution: Multiple receptor types form a stereotyped molecular topography with receptors localized to domains receiving cell-type-specific inputs. Developmental observations suggest receptors or their complexes with other membrane proteins help determine input patterns. A transmembrane protein associated with a subset of restricted synapses is required for synapse formation.
ocar.future_work: They propose that mechanisms placing receptors precisely provide a molecular cartography specifying dendritic synaptic patterns.

summaries.beginner: A cell can listen with several kinds of chemical receivers, and those receivers may sit only where particular partners connect. This paper maps those receivers onto identified fly motion-sensing cells and finds a highly regular layout, plus one helper protein needed to build a subset of contacts.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuron (2024), Sanfilippo and colleagues combine epitope-tagged neurotransmitter receptors, expansion light-sheet microscopy, and electron-microscopy connectomics in Drosophila motion-sensitive neurons. Receptor subtypes occupy stereotyped dendritic domains matched to specific input types. A transmembrane protein at a spatially restricted synapse class is required for those synapses to form, supporting a developmental role for receptor complexes in specifying inputs.
summaries.advanced: Molecular topography is shown for the studied motion-sensitive neurons, not all fly cell types. Requirement of the transmembrane protein is genetic for that synapse subset. Catalog method tag is light-sheet; electron microscopy is used as connectomic context in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: A cell can listen with several kinds of chemical receivers, and those receivers may sit only where particular partners connect. This paper maps those receivers onto identified fly motion-sensing cells and finds a highly regular layout, plus one helper protein needed to build a subset of contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Neuropeptides control neuronal activity and behavior in all animals. C. elegans’ compact nervous system has been a primary model for how neuropeptide networks are organized.
ocar.challenge: A synthesis of evolutionary conservation, molecular expression, receptor–ligand interactions, and system-wide organization of worm neuropeptide pathways was needed as other organisms begin to chart peptide networks.
ocar.action: Watteyne and colleagues review recent work mapping conservation, expression, receptor–ligand pairing, and organism-wide organization of C. elegans neuropeptide signaling, plus in vivo studies of circuit motifs and spatiotemporal range.
ocar.resolution: They describe general insights into peptidergic circuit motifs and the range of peptidergic transmission. They argue the C. elegans neuropeptidergic connectome can serve as a prototype for organization and signaling dynamics at organismal scale.
ocar.future_work: Efforts to chart peptide networks in other organisms can use this prototype.

summaries.beginner: Besides wired contacts, nerve cells send peptide messages that can act more widely and slowly. This review gathers how those peptide systems are built and used in the roundworm, as a guide for other animals.
summaries.intermediate: In Genetics (2024), Watteyne, Chudinova, Ripoll-Sánchez, Schafer, and Beets review the C. elegans neuropeptide signaling network from structure to behavior. They cover evolutionary conservation, molecular expression, receptor–ligand maps, and system-wide organization. In vivo studies are synthesized for peptidergic circuit motifs and the spatiotemporal range of transmission, presenting the worm peptidergic connectome as a prototype for other animals.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new ligand screen. Prototype status is an argument for transfer, not a demonstration in another species. Insights from in vivo studies are synthesized rather than re-measured here.

plain_language_summary: Besides wired contacts, nerve cells send peptide messages that can act more widely and slowly. This review gathers how those peptide systems are built and used in the roundworm, as a guide for other animals.

ocar.opportunity: A complete fruit-fly nerve-cord connectome—the first for an animal that can walk or fly—needs systematic names and types to be navigable and comparable to experiments. Hierarchical annotations linked to literature would make the map usable.
ocar.challenge: Without systematic cell types spanning the midline and segments, the ventral nerve cord volume is hard to analyze programmatically or to match to prior genetics and physiology.
ocar.action: Marin and colleagues categorise and name nearly all neurons in the adult male Drosophila nerve-cord connectome (companion reconstruction by Takemura et al., 2023), defining types for sensory, intrinsic, ascending, and non-motor efferent neurons, matching serial homologs, and assigning sensory modalities.
ocar.resolution: Larval-born neurons of a hemilineage generally share a neurotransmitter, though earlier-born neurons often differ, and over 35% of intrinsic, ascending, and non-motor efferent neurons match across segments. The authors assign a sensory modality to over 5,000 sensory neurons, find layered organisation likely matching peripheral topography, and illustrate sensory circuits from programmatic analysis of the complete ventral nerve cord. Annotations are released via neuPrint, Clio, and dedicated tools, and underpin a companion analysis of descending input and motor output.
ocar.future_work: Annotations are intended as the basis for structure of descending input and motor output and for ongoing programmatic analysis.

summaries.beginner: A complete wiring map of the fly’s nerve cord is only useful if every cell has a name and a type that match what experiments already know. This preprint does that naming job and finds repeating cell families along the body and a layered layout of sensory inputs.
summaries.intermediate: On bioRxiv (2024 record), Marin and colleagues systematically annotate the complete adult male Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectome from the companion Takemura et al. (2023) reconstruction. Hierarchical types cover sensory, intrinsic, ascending, and non-motor efferent cells, with serial homologs and hemilineage neurotransmitter rules (and exceptions for earlier-born neurons). They match over 35% of those central classes across segments, assign modality to over 5,000 sensory neurons, and release annotations on neuPrint and Clio.
summaries.advanced: Motor-neuron typing and descending/motor analyses are in companion papers. ‘Nearly all neurons’ still leaves some untyped. Serial matching at over 35% means most cells are not serially assigned. Catalog method is neuPrint as the delivery platform.

plain_language_summary: A complete wiring map of the fly’s nerve cord is only useful if every cell has a name and a type that match what experiments already know. This preprint does that naming job and finds repeating cell families along the body and a layered layout of sensory inputs.
